This paper investigates two-stage robust optimization problems with binary uncertainties at the second stage, taking into account various scenario-based formulations and their dual problems. This article delves into the world of common rings, including p-adic rings, matrix rings, matrix units, Weyl algebras, and Artin algebras, to establish the underlying numbers that p-bounding in these contexts relies upon. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first comprehensive attempt to explore the Cohen p-bounding numbers in the realm of rings, and it builds on initial findings in the literature. Alongside the main results, interesting corollaries and applications have been identified, particularly in the context of Weyl algebras and quasi-Frobenius rings. One of the key outcomes of this research reveals that Cohen p-bounding in matrix units $\operatorname{Mat}_n(R)$ over a ring R equals the p-bounding number of R. This surprising discovery leads to remarkable implications and a fundamental question regarding Cohen p-bounding in matrix units. Additionally, the article explores Cohen p-bounding in Weyl algebras, ultimately showing that it equals the p-bounding number of its underlying ring. Consequently, the authors pose a central inquiry: determine the p-bounding number of Weyl algebra $A_n(K)$. The primary objective of machine learning (ML) based solutions is to develop general and adaptable models that can apply throughout a given domain without relying on specific instances. However, in reality, most ML models tend to perform poorly when encountering instances outside of their training data due to over-reliance on familiar patterns. This issue is particularly pronounced in computer vision, where most models struggle with conceptually complex and often adversarial inputs. To mitigate this problem, researchers are seeking ML models that can withstand and learn from challenging inputs characteristic of complex domains. This work is focused on proposing and exploring an existing method, known as Adversarial Training, and evaluating its effectiveness in promoting organically resilient ML models. To this end, we introduce a benchmark dataset designed to assess a model's ability to handle and learn from adversarial inputs characteristic of domains like computer vision, where conceptually complex and often global patterns need to be inferred. Our solution, dubbed ADVS, is a simple and efficient approach that leverages the low-frequency components of images to create more challenging and conceptually rich inputs. Our experiments demonstrate that ADVS is effective in promoting organically resilient ML models, and our code and benchmarking tools are openly available to support further research in this area. We anticipate that our research will help inform and guide future developments in this area. Additionally, we discuss potential applications and extensions of this method, including its use in boosting model robustness against adversarial attacks. We confirm through a series of numerical experiments performed with the pyent package that the analytical and numerical results presented in this research hold true in practice.

We find that the new method retains the four-parton tagging's high misclassification rate for four-parton tops while significantly reducing the misclassification rate for two-parton tops relative to the original algorithm. We analyze the improved method's performance using Shapley values, which reveal that jet properties contribute more substantially to tagging outcomes than before and that the dominant factor varies across topologies. Furthermore, when treating top tagging as a collaborative effort of individual jet properties, the interpretability of the algorithm is increased. Additionally, when calculating the Shapley values for the entire top tagging process, the relative importance of each taglet's contribution is determined, and it is observed that only a few taglets are essential for the tagging's overall success. We also explore the implications of taglets overlapping in space and tagking in calorimetry, and demonstrate that the Shapley values allow for the identification of physics principles governing tagging in these scenarios. The standard approach, however, may result in large storage demands and non-uniformly distributed past experiences that may not provide sufficient insight into more challenging states. In order to mitigate these issues, a novel experience replay strategy called Past Experience Focus (PEF) was developed. The system works by prioritizing the storage of experiences based on their novelty, effectively allowing past interactions to be focused on those that were previously under-represented. Integration of PEF with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) has been shown to yield improved results by reducing variance and speed up convergence in scenarios such as DQN, DDPG and QRDQN without requiring any modifications to these established frameworks. Furthermore, a combination of PEF and actor-critic collaboration achieved state-of-the-art results in several benchmark tasks including additional challenging domains in the OpenAI Gym library. The code for PEF has been made publicly available to facilitate future research. The results of our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach and provide a solid foundation for exploring new research directions with PEF. In order to assess the efficacy of GPEF, a series of numerical experiments were conducted to evaluate its performance across multiple experience replay-based algorithms to validate its effectiveness. Certain specific types of tsunami waves generated by asteroid impacts can travel long distances at speeds significantly higher than typical tsunami waves, allowing them to cross entire ocean basins in time frames relevant for disaster preparedness and response planning. Dispersive effects caused by varying ocean depths or densities can further accelerate these waves. Due to their distinct characteristics, we recommend a unique approach when modeling their propagation. A method that effectively splits the simulation domain into local areas with different spatial resolutions can help maintain a high level of accuracy while ensuring the simulation remains efficient by keeping the total number of elements relatively low. We introduce an optimized version of the discontinuous Galerkin method that allows local refinement of the simulation, and verify its accuracy through a range of test cases including non-dispersive tsunami wave simulations. Additionally, we incorporate a version of the shallow water equations optimized for fast and basic tsunami wave propagation. Lastly, we showcase the application of our method to a scenario where a high-dispersive tsunami wave is triggered by an asteroid collision and then transmitted across a variable-depth ocean to a coastal solver for risk assessment. Dispersive effects can cause significant modifications to the tsunami wave profile by the time it reaches land, and accurately modeled using our approach, which highlights the importance of incorporating these mechanisms in asteroid-generated tsunami simulations. These simulations, in turn, offer a more reliable basis for informed decision-making and emergency planning in cases of asteroid-generated tsunamis. The main aim of the NLP field, HyperExpan: Classification, is to predict target 
classifications for given input sequences from a limited set of choices by 
disentangling the representation space into a hyperbolic structure with a
limited number of nodes, based on pre-trained language models' initial suggestions.
Previous research indicates that hyperbolic representation learning yields 
improved results in tasks related to graph data and can create efficient 
representation schemes for complex datasets. Nevertheless, the potential of 
hyperbolic learning in expanding classification labels has not been thoroughly 
explored, even though it could be beneficial in domains such as text, where it 
could lead to cost savings by avoiding label annotation. Our model, HyperExpan, 
achieves this goal by training a rotating graph with a limited set of nodes, 
utilizing the initial suggestions of language models as a starting point. 
Additionally, we introduce new metrics to assess the quality of representation 
schemes in hyperbolic space. On datasets such as SST-2, IMDB, and Subj, 
HyperExpan shows comparable or better performance than other competing methods, 
including a significant improvement in accuracy on the Subj dataset, with the 
source code available at:  https://github.com/andreafan/fb-rotating-hyperbolic-learning. Further research is required to study hyperbolic learning in domain adaptation scenarios. 

Please note that this work was originally published at the 2022 IEEE Workshop on Deep Learning for Audio Speech and Image Processing (DL-ASIP).

To resolve this uncertainty, researchers created mock catalogs of two different populations and compared them to real data. We develop a class of nonlocal stochastic models tailored to capture coherent structures in turbulence, beginning with a detailed representation of their linearized versions and then expanding to include nonlinear dynamics. This regime of turbulence is characterized by quasi-particles with distinct velocities that exhibit coherent behavior only under certain conditions, and we derive a corresponding stochastic propagation based on statistical coherence. The resulting pattern of motion is illustrated by a concrete example of turbulent gas molecules coalescing into coherent particles, and we discuss how the degree of coherence affects both dynamics and coherence. Ultimately, we identify a specific case that yields a localized particle-like behavior even in the absence of coherence, and we examine the implications for both phase space dynamics and coherence. Along the way, we develop novel methods for analyzing stochastic dynamics, including a general approach to deriving nonlinear stochastic propagators and a detailed examination of quasi-particle behavior in one-dimensional settings. The underlying mathematical structure of these stochastic models is shown to be rooted in noncommutative geometry, and we discuss how the resulting patterns of motion can be understood from a geometric perspective. The chapter concludes by exploring the relevance of these stochastic models to a variety of physical and biological situations, including the coalescence of dust particles, the emergence of schools of fish, and the migration of cancer cells. In the accompanying notes, we delve deeper into several mathematical topics related to these stochastic models, including the Poincaré-Lefshetz duality, the Chern character formula, and the Kolmogorov equation for coalescing quasi-particles. The chapter and accompanying notes assume only a basic understanding of stochastic models and turbulence, and everything else is developed from first principles. We introduce {\sc Flexible Scattering Phenomenology} (${\cal FS}^2$pho), a suite of programs and macros tailored to address phenomenological scattering processes in a flexible and efficient manner. The primary focus is on phenomenology associated with top-quark pair production with high-energy colliders in mind. These include partonic scattering processes, associated distributions, observables, and their corresponding cumulative sums, enabling phenomenological analysis and optimization. The implementation of these tools exploits the flexibility of {\sc FlexTAP}, a transcendental numerical analysis library, to address distributions and observables with one argument, and {\sc FlexIntTAP}, a transcendental numerical analysis library for distributions and observables with multiple arguments. The presented methods and implementation details enable a dramatic reduction in computational time compared to conventional Monte Carlo techniques. The {\scFS}^2pho suite operates as a phenomenological "black-box" and is not reliant on physical interpretations of the input parameters. The package is designed to be easily extensible for a broad range of scattering phenomenology applications. As a validation, we outline the methodology for deriving scattering phenomenology distributions from a set of fundamental physical parameters, specifically focusing on the top-quark charge. The implementation details and validation results are provided for programs written in {\sc C} with {\sc C}AMALIA} and Python with {\sc PyFormex}. A comprehensive {\scFS}^2pho suite consisting of source code, executables, and configuration files is made available through a public repository. The repository includes a pre-compiled {\scFS}^2pho suite along with a comprehensive set of configuration files and input parameters, enabling users to run the phenomenological scattering analysis. The suite is accessible via https://github.com/FlexiblePheno/${\calFS}^2$pho. The provided {\scFS}^2pho suite constitutes an essential contribution to scattering phenomenology analysis and optimization software. The extensive suite of efficient scattering analysis tools, combined with flexible phenomenological analysis capabilities, will greatly benefit high-energy physics phenomenology and optimization research. The present work is part of a broader effort to develop and disseminate Flexible Pheno software tools. The tools and associated information presented within this dissertation are distributed without restriction, and the user base is intended to expand beyond high-energy physics and include a broader scientific community. The corresponding dissemination channels include the {\scFS}^2pho suite's GitHub page and the author's professional profile on the ArXiv HEP Announcements hub

This paper presents a comprehensive thermal analysis of a blackbody in the presence of Casimir's effect, with the aim of examining how electromagnetic vacuum fluctuations affect blackbody thermodynamics. To achieve this, two systems consisting of two parallel plates separated by a distance $L$ are considered, one containing a blackbody and the other an oscillating mirror. A canonical quantization method is used to derive the free energy of each system and evaluate its entropy. Comparison of the entropies reveals that the free energy of the blackbody increases by a surface term proportional to $1/L^2$, indicating that the Casimir effect exerts a pressure on the blackbody. Furthermore, the analysis shows that the Casimir effect introduces a non-zero temperature-dependent pressure in the thermal equilibrium state of the blackbody. To maintain thermodynamic equilibrium, the blackbody must compensate for the effect by adjusting its energy distribution. Depending on the value of $L$, the Casimir effect can either decrease or increase the blackbody's entropy, with the entropy being proportional to $1/L^2$. These findings align with the third law of thermodynamics, with the asymptotic behavior of the entropy as $L \to 0$ dependent on whether $T \neq 0$ or $T = 0$. In addition, when $T = 0$, the analysis shows that the Casimir effect introduces a zero-temperature pressure on the blackbody. Finally, the analysis highlights that the Casimir effect may compromise the uniqueness of the blackbody radiation. By examining the possible distribution of energy among space components, the analysis shows that the Casimir effect may lead to multiple radiative states that satisfy the equipartite condition at $T = 0$. With increasing temperature, the energy associated with the transverse modes is found to be independent of the system's dimensions, suggesting that the Casimir effect may result in a thermal phase transition in the blackbody radiation. To determine the specific phase transition, the analysis identifies an critical temperature $T_c$ at which the transition occurs, with the behavior of energy distribution below and above this temperature indicating two possible radiative states. By evaluating the energy distributions below and above $T_c$, the analysis shows that the Casimir effect may induce a nonequivalent and nonequivalent distribution of energy, with the energy associated with the longitudinal modes being independent of system's dimensions and increasing linearly with temperature, respectively. These findings suggest that the Casimir effect may cause a failure of the Rayleigh-Jeans law in the UV regime

It leverages a novel Normal Distribution Transform depiction (NDT) descriptor, employing a Transformer model for cross-localization between different datasets. Utilizing 3D point clouds, the NDT descriptor captures localized descriptor variations, unlike previous methods that relied on global features. A multi-scale Transformer architecture follows, facilitating the selection of multiple localized descriptors across different scales. Subsequently, a support vector regression module performs precise metric localization. Experimental results demonstrate exceptional performance on well-known datasets, surpassing state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, the framework exhibits generalization and efficient processing of large-scale datasets, localizing across various scales and training conditions without compromising performance. All code and data is openly available on GitHub. The framework's successful implementation enables cross-domain localization without training and demonstrates a new paradigm for metric localization. Notably, the proposed method sets a new benchmark for localization across large-scale datasets, achieving state-of-the-art performance. A novel analysis of the NDT descriptor's performance is also provided, showing that a multi-scale Transformer architecture is essential for capturing scale information. Resting-state functional MRI data display robust, spontaneous neural connections known as functional networks, whose structures can be identified with multisite datasets that bring together data from various research sites. By combining data from six research sites, this study examines how statistical measures of network edges affect prediction accuracy in identifying sites based on network characteristics. Using multivariate Bayesian classification, it is found that center-specific network features and long-distance, between-site connections can distinguish individual research sites, while short-distance, within-site connections serve as a control. Notably, prediction efficiency is enhanced when all sites have equal data availability; however, this requires careful consideration of network edge statistical properties to mitigate the impact of uneven data. With data availability ratios as input, a multivariate classification approach still achieves substantial classification accuracy for most scenarios. Finally, prediction results are consistent when using network edge strength or topological measurements, underscoring the role of data availability in identifying site-specific functional network characteristics. These findings may have significant implications for predictive modeling in neuroimaging. In systems utilizing distinct signal outputs, known as beeping networks, a centralized naming system is employed where a special node, the coordinator, generates unique sequences of signals upon receiving requests from other nodes. This setup allows identifying devices based on their connection time, despite no clock being available. Yet, utilizing beeping channels to communicate via multi-bit data comes with a significant cost due to limited bandwidth and the risk of package collisions. To optimize connection management, a proposing node initially sends a one-bit request to either join the network or leave it, with the coordinator responding positively or negatively to the request. This paper presents an innovative, power-saving approach, based on randomized requests, allowing nodes either enter the network or leave it without requiring coordinator involvement in the request process. This solution aligns with the requirements of self-stabilization, meaning it can function reliably even in scenarios where the network is disturbed and nodes randomly join or disconnect from the network. We provide an in-depth analysis of the coordinator's state and offer an accurate upper limit on the expected waiting time for a node to either join or leave the network. Furthermore, a numerical study demonstrates that this system remains highly efficient even for a substantial number of nodes in the network. This optimization is achieved by reducing the maximum waiting time and, more importantly, decreases the total time by a factor proportional to the number of nodes in the network, leading to significantly improved power savings. The proposed solution is implemented and experimentally validated using THMag modules. Validation results confirm that this approach efficiently decreases power consumption by a factor proportional to the number of nodes in the network. Finally, a practical application of this solution to a real-world scenario involving a robotics competition demonstrates its practicality and effectiveness. To address the requirement of maintaining a balanced robot distribution, we developed a beeping-based system to optimize connection management and, as a result, maintain a fair robot distribution while enabling real-time online monitoring and efficient online scheduling. This solution is efficient because it maintains a balanced distribution by allowing robots to enter the network or leave it using randomized requests, which do not require coordinator involvement and lead to a significant improvement in power consumption by a factor proportional to the number of robots in the network. As a result, this solution received positive feedback from the competition organizers. Code-mixed texts, which are prevalent in social media, are a combination of languages written without using language codes or translation. They can be considered as intermediate forms between fully mixed and pure languages. Due to their unique nature, existing machine learning models may not perform well on code-mixed data. A particular challenge arises in handling texts that contain words from multiple languages in positions that are relative to other words in the text. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach called Transition Point based Dynamic and Relative Positional Encoding (PETO). This method aims to capture the positional significance of words in code-mixed texts by assigning weights to the transition points between languages. To optimize performance, we incorporate a language identification step and employ positional encoding to represent the positional significance of words. PETO has been evaluated on two code-mixed datasets, XELS-RC and TAMIL-RC, and compared with state-of-the-art models. Our experiments show that incorporating transition points as positional features leads to significant performance improvements, which range from 2% to 20% in terms of ROUGE metrics. Furthermore, our approach outperforms existing methods in zero-shot text classification tasks by achieving an F1 score of 0.714 on a Tamil-English dataset. The source code for PESTO is available at https://github.com/ashishch19/PESTO. Our research indicates that incorporating transition points as positional features is a valuable approach to handling code-mixed data, which can lead to substantial performance improvements. Moreover, it offers a novel framework for modeling positional dependencies in fully mixed texts. Extensive experimentation on various code-mixed datasets has been conducted to validate the generalizability of our approach. To the best of our knowledge, our research makes a significant contribution to the machine learning community by addressing the positional challenges in code-mixed data through a pioneering technique. PESTO has the potential to inspire further research on positional modeling in mixed language texts and enhance the machine learning community's understanding of positional modeling in code-mixed data. Additionally, it can benefit researchers working on language processing for code-mixed data and enhance their knowledge of positional modeling in code-mixed data. We examined how different isotopes affect the characteristics of H$_{3}$S as a superconductor under varying pressures. Using a tight-binding model, we calculated the band structure of H$_{3}$S along the M-D axis to $\Gamma$ point, taking into account the effect of a van Hove singularity. Our results suggest a direct transition from a normal metal to a superconductor at the critical pressure $p_c= 160$ GPa, regardless of isotope effects. At a lower pressure of 100 GPa, the same scenario occurs, but with an exception - superconductivity only arises if an isotopic variation is considered. Using second-order perturbation theory and BCS theory, we determined the critical temperature $\Delta T_c_{isotop}$ resulting from isotopic effects at 160 GPa. Additionally, we discovered that the presence of a van Hove singularity amplifies the isotope effect by a factor of 2. We also determined the critical pressure $p_{vHS}$ where the isotope effect on $T_c$ becomes significant, happening at 140 GPa. Our findings provide a basis for understanding why H$_{3}$S as a superconductor has not yet been discovered, taking into account pressure, isotopes, and the presence of a van Hove singularity. Furthermore, at a lower pressure of 100 GPa, the same scenario occurs, but with an exception - superconductivity only arises if an isotopic variation is considered. Our model also indicates that the van Hove singularity at a lower energy scale has a more pronounced effect compared to the primary van Hove singularity. Our findings also suggest that the superconducting properties of materials like MgB$_2$ and BaB$_6$ are unlikely to be significantly influenced by isotopes. We also determined that to achieve similar effects on $T_c$ as observed in La, Ba, and Ce hydrides, an enormous amount of pressure ($p \sim  300$ GPa) would be required. Our model also indicates that to achieve a similar enhancement of $T_c$ as observed in La, Ba, and Ce hydrides, an enormous number of isotopes ($N \sim  200$) would be required. Our findings also provide a basis for understanding why H$_{3}$S as a superconductor has not yet been discovered, taking into account pressure, isotopes, and the presence of a van Hove singularity.

In motion planning with spatial constraints, algorithms process map data and physical limitations to generate optimal paths. We focus on a scenario where a mobile robot navigates through an ever-changing environment without a pre-existing map. Our goal is for the robot to safely and efficiently plottwo-dimensional paths around dynamic obstacles. To achieve this, we introduce a novel technique - spatial limitation creation - that enables a mobile robot to self-construct a map while navigating through an uncharted environment. This method employs a level-set map data structure and an innovative constraint-based map updating approach to ensure the robot's map remains consistent with its surroundings. We propose a sequential map data association algorithm to determine the optimal spatial constraints for the robot's current state. Our approach combines a gradient-based path optimization strategy with spatial constraint determination, leveraging numerical solving and dynamic programming to address the problem. We validate the efficacy of our method through simulations on various cases and demonstrate its practical application in a mobile robot platform. Additionally, we compare the performance of our method with existing map-building and constraint-based planners in different settings. Our method outperforms other approaches in terms of path length, path speed, and computational efficiency in both random and real-world scenarios. Moreover, we demonstrate that our method adapts to diverse computational budgets by showcasing a trade-off between computation time and path length. Finally, we demonstrate the practical implementation of our method on a mobile robot platform. Our method successfully generates optimal paths in real-time on the robot platform. Our experimental results reveal that the robot's computed paths closely align with those obtained offline using the same motion planner. To assess the fairness of our method, we performed a pairwise comparison test and found that the majority of human observers prefer the paths computed by our method over those generated by an alternative online motion planner. In contrast, some human observers prefer the paths generated by the alternative motion planner. Our comprehensive evaluation of our method confirms its effectiveness in navigating and mapping dynamic environments in a mobile robot system. Our method successfully navigates through an average of 87% of environments without human intervention and achieves a satisfactory path rating from humans for the remaining 13% of cases. In particular, our method achieves an average path length that is at most 5% longer than the optimal offline path, as determined by offline motion planning. Our method establishes a dynamic and adaptive system that balances computational resource usage and system performance in mobile robots. This research targets visual relocalization in dynamic environments using 3D surfel mapping. A novel framework is introduced, consisting of a live system and a pre-trained network, where both utilize surfel features. The pre-trained network is used for localization and initial mapping, while the live system applies online learning to navigate unfamiliar areas with minimal new data. A unique feature representation based on generalized spherical convolution is developed, compatible with omnidirectional cameras. This feature representation is specifically designed for scene understanding and learned feature development. The framework combines a geometric localization module with a photometric module for enhanced accuracy. Furthermore, the paper introduces an online learning method that adapts features from a few initial images to increase the live system's resilience to changes in environment lighting conditions. The proposed framework features real-time performance and is simple to implement. It surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of accuracy, with a 95% achievement over 10 frames per second when used with a single CPU on the Malaga dataset and outperforms other localization techniques. The method demonstrates online and offline resilience to challenging lighting conditions, with online performance remaining stable across all scenarios. A related project and code are available on GitHub at https://github.com/eth-siai/3D-Surfel-VLRL. The version of the code used for this research can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.754444. Additionally, the accompanying data can be found at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.754444.

The study focuses on random measures that are consistent in the weak sense and converge to a quantum process. Degrading matrix-valued measures to scalar ones results in the formation of new family of measures, the key is to establish their weak algebraic convergence to a quantum process. By leveraging the link between quantum processes and stochastic evolution equations, solving this equation with a matrix-valued measure as the starting point allows for the generation of a new family of measures that are converging to a quantum process. This paper introduces a Dict-BERT model for pre-training a language model using a comprehensive dictionary with nuanced word representations. By assuming that words with similar meanings have relative meanings, we can refine the model's understanding of words during the pre-training phase. Our innovative method, which utilizes a dictionary to detect word similarities, can be combined with existing BERT models for improved performance. Experimental results show that the Dict-BERT model achieved a new state-of-the-art accuracy of 92.8% on the WordSim-235 dataset and outperformed other baseline models in various NLP tasks, including glue and sst. Notably, we found that using a dictionary with 23,363 entries was sufficient for the Dict-BERT model to reach its full potential, which is significantly more efficient than other existing word similarity models. Additionally, we open-source the Dict-BERT model on GitHub at https://github.com/SD-SEM-DL/Dict-BERT. Further evaluation demonstrated that the Dict-BERT model excelled in various aspects, which are discussed further in Section 6. Ultimately, we hope this model can enhance the efficacy of downstream NLP tasks and contribute to improved word representations in language models. Moreover, we can use this model to discover new word relationships in various domains, which can aid human comprehension, as illustrated in Section 7.0. Finally, we provide an updated version of the Dict-BERT model called Dict-Electra that outperforms Dict-BERT in most tasks and achieves improved efficiency by using existing language models as a starting point, which are discussed in Section 8.0. Interestingly, we found that using dictionaries for language models is a highly effective and efficient approach that can enhance both model performance and efficiency. Ultimately, we hope this work can contribute to the advancement of language models in the future. Moreover, we have updated the code and models to reflect the latest changes, which can be found at https://github.com/SD-SEM-DL/Dict-BERT-Dictionary-Based-Language-Model. The effectiveness of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) heavily relies on sufficient network node labels, but these are often scarce in real-world scenarios. To mitigate this issue, pseudo-labeling can be employed to virtualize extra supervision by identifying and assigning the most likely label to each node. Nevertheless, pseudo-labeling may introduce errors in the supervised pipeline and exacerbate difficulties when only a limited number of labels are available. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel pseudo-labeling framework for improving GNN performance under data scarcity. This approach, called EnLightGNN, combines multiple pseudo-labeling techniques with a specialized error correction method. EnLightGNN applies multi-view pseudo-labeling to increase diversity and then refines the results by considering both node importance and neighboring errors in the network. This technique has been tested with eight datasets, including both synthetic and real-world examples, with results showing significant performance improvements, particularly up to 9.7% accuracy increase when only a small number of labels are available. This research introduces a Bayesian framework for choosing optimal chain event graphs in Bayesian networks by using maximum a posteriori estimation. Our contribution is a systematic way to apply Bayesian frameworks to chain event graphs, in contrast to existing literature which focuses on parameter estimation. Specifically, we demonstrate that the posterior distribution of a chain event graph has the property of exchangeability, allowing the application of Danaeiyan and Razzaghi's theorem to establish a concentration inequality for the Bayesian risk. This result showcases that the Bayesian estimator is asymptotically minimax with the Bayesian risk converging at an algebraic rate for a large number of observations. We also present numerical illustrations that demonstrate the superiority of our Bayesian approach compared to a frequentist method on real-world datasets. Furthermore, we propose a practical Monte Carlo algorithm for the Bayesian MAP estimation of chain event graphs. Our method is evaluated using simulated datasets of various sizes and on actual datasets from the fields of medicine and social science. We also compare it to a frequentist method on actual datasets from medicine and social science. In addition to the methodological contributions, we present an extension of the chain event graph model that can accommodate missing data by assuming that some variables do not interact with each other. Our main algorithm can be applied to this extended model as well. We apply the Bayesian MAP algorithm to real-world datasets, including the TD2002 dataset from the National Institutes of Health-funded Treatment of Depression Collaborative Clinic dataset and the SUDBURY12 dataset from the Canadian Institute for Advanced Study on Social Science Data. The results show that the proposed algorithm is scalable for large datasets with thousands of samples and that it can handle complex chain event graphs with hundreds of nodes. We also observe that the Bayesian estimator performs well even when the prior distribution is unknown. Our method can be used as an offline tool to evaluate the performance of other estimators. We also show that the Bayesian estimator achieves the lowest Bayesian risk in our numerical illustrations. This study introduces Unruly Shifts as a movement strategy in unsupervised wall following robots.  A wall following robot executes an unwavering right turn at every distance, with the right turn radius being determined by the robot's measurement of the wall at that point.  This simple algorithm yields a path that deviates from the ideal wall hugging path in certain sections but in a predictable manner.  This predictable deviation enables a partnership between two or more robots following this path to create a collective movement that mimics animal pac-making behaviors.  Our simulation of this algorithm on 2 and 3 dimensional spaces reveals that the resulting patterns do not exhibit periodic behavior but the disturbance caused by one robot's path can be anticipated by others.  Furthermore, our research demonstrates that the potential for synchronization through collective movement is not solely dependent on the predictable nature of the path but can also arise from the paths created by the deviations caused by the divergence from the ideal path.  In addition, our study also explores the potential for generating spiral patterns that resemble plant phyllotaxis through 3 or more robots following each other.  This behavior in 3 or more robots can be controlled by introducing variations in the measurement of the wall made by the robots.  One key advantage of our algorithm is its independence from the capabilities and design of the robots and can therefore be considered as an inherent property of the system when analyzed at a sufficient level of complexity.  Our research also delves into the possibility of self-replication through the paths created by the robots.  Lastly, our study outlines a number of potential applications including the creation of robotic flowers, the simulation of plant growth, the design of robotic gaits, the generation of artistic patterns and the development of robotic gauges.  Our research suggests that the potential for self-organization and collective movement in systems with simple algorithms can be vast and far from what is currently understood.  Our work also highlights the need to explore the boundary between order and disorder in the behavior of autonomous systems and to distinguish clearly between the concepts of determinism and predictability.  Our research further suggests that the border between these concepts may be discovered within the messiness of real world systems.  Our study also delves into the possibility of uncovering emergent behavior in systems where the actions of the agents are not clearly defined.  Our research further suggests that the ideal path may be replaced by a standard of acceptable deviation from the ideal path. We present a quantum mechanical model of a self-organizing statistical system that generates SLE k loop evolutions when k exceeds 4/3. The model consists of mutually interacting quantum disks in 2D space, where each disk represents an SLE k evolvement. It is shown that conformal fusion of these disks produces the desired SLE k loop growth for k greater than or equal to 4/3. Furthermore, we found that the probability distribution of the loop radius in our model adheres to Schramm's universal law associated with Wasserstein-2 distance as loop length increases. This is analogous to findings by Ocampo and Miller regarding CFT biquadratic interface evolution driven by conformal fusion of quantum droplets. Our model is non-perturbative and stands as a new example of a self-organizing critical system that reaches self-organization under suitable parameter conditions, thus offering a novel, explicit, and rigorous framework for SLE k loop evolution when k exceeds 4/3. For k equal to 4/3, equal to 4, and equal to 4 plus 3 times the square root of 6, we found that critical probability yields either beta equal to 3, 6, and 18 respectively, under suitable scaling, thus providing an exact beta value for each of the three respective SLE k types. The model is studied under the condition that quantum disks have a nonzero average radius. This is in contrast to the SLE k loop evolution model developed by Dubedat, which is based on holomorphic quantum graphs. Our approach is similar to the SLE k curve evolution model developed by Kozlov and Miller. A model proposes that a primordial black hole of enormous mass can be formed through the collapse of a quantum fluctuation-induced singular object known as the running curvaton, characterised by a decaying scalar field wavelength. The CTR-SOLO formulation is equivalent to a quadratic optimization problem with linear constraints, making it solvable via convex relaxation and reduction to a linearly constrained elastic net optimization problem. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the CTR-SOLO approach against alternative models, including elastic net, Lasso, and Adaboost. Recent research highlights the effectiveness of artificially generated headlines in social engineering, which can be leveraged by mechanically crafted headlines in phishing scams. Notably, phishing attacks have increasingly employed headline suggestions from language models, whose potential impact has yet to be systematically evaluated. This study aims to fill this gap by investigating the effectiveness of publicly available transformer-based language models in generating plausible headline suggestions. We also explored the potential of utilizing these models in phishing attacks and compared their performance against state-of-the-art transformer-based models, notably BERT. The experiment revealed that a specific model, T5, excels in creating realistic headline suggestions, outperforming BERT. Furthermore, our controlled phishing attack using 1,000 generated headlines successfully tricked 12% of participants into revealing sensitive credentials. While the numbers are currently not impressive, our findings offer valuable insights into the vulnerabilities presented by publicly accessible language models, which can be exploited by socially engineered phishing attacks. We also outline practical measures to prevent such phishing attempts and motivate the development of language models that can detect mechanically crafted headlines used in phishing scams. We present a novel, autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network model that effectively diversifies portfolio distributions. By using a conditional autoencoder to eliminate irrelevant data dimension variables, we downsize high-return, undiversified portfolio setups. Next, our GAN trainer instructs a generator to create new, more diversified portfolios in a training data space with reduced dimensions. We have successfully tested our method on actual investor fund manager data, achieving substantial improvements in portfolio diversification within both the training and non-training data sets. Moreover, our model outperforms established portfolio optimization techniques in various evaluations. When assessing the model's performance using both numerical measures and visualizations, we found that our method results in more diversified and profitable portfolios according to both metrics. Therefore, we believe that our novel GAN approach offers a valuable, efficient solution to the portfolio diversification challenge for both academic and industry professionals. It has the added benefit of being easy to use, as it requires no prior knowledge of either machine learning or finance. All that is needed is a set of labeled data and a specified number of output data points, after which the generator can produce diversified portfolio distributions on its own. Subsequent portfolio evaluations can be performed automatically without any further human intervention. For hypergraphs with vertex sets of size at most k, their tensor product is defined using the Kronecker product, resulting in a k-dimensional grid matrix. The purpose of this study is to explore the properties of hypergraph tensor products. These include the commutative property, irreducibility, eigenvalue properties, and algebraic closure. Notably, the study demonstrates that the tensor product of hypergraphs retains essential features, such as the connectivity and simplicity characteristics. Furthermore, the study involves analyzing the eigenvalues of the tensor product, revealing that certain eigenvalues related to the Lovász number and the stability number reside on the principal diagonal. As a result, the study provides conditions under which the tensor product's eigenvalues do not vanish. This research also shows that the tensor product's irreducibility depends on the properties of the individual hypergraphs. Lastly, the study illustrates that the tensor product's spectra capture information about the properties of the individual hypergraphs, particularly the retention of the eigenvalues related to the Lovász number and the stability number. These findings contribute significantly to hypergraph theory, offering new insights and approaches to understanding hypergraphs. The study includes numerical examples to facilitate better understanding and presentation of the results. The study concludes by introducing novel research questions. In clinical trials for Alzheimer's and progressive diseases tracked with continuous data, the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is used to compare distributions, which is particularly significant as it doesn't violate assumptions. A problem with this approach is that it doesn't utilize all gathered data, which can result in reduced statistical power. To rectify this issue, a novel method using natural cubic splines is introduced, designed to examine statistical differences in continuous data distributions in Alzheimer's clinical trials. This method is compared to the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov approach through simulations and practical application. The results indicate that the new method yields improved statistical power with comparable p-value distributions. A case study involving the CRESENT trial is also conducted to illustrate the usefulness of this approach in evaluating treatment effects. The statistical analysis from this case study suggests no substantial treatment effects were found for patients receiving solanezumab or lanadelumab in comparison to the placebo, which was consistent across multiple comparisons including the novel method, the augmented Kolmogorov-Smirnov approach, and other conventional analyses. The proposed method is presented in an R package called ncsAlz, which is available at GitHub. The data from the CRESENT trial used in this case study are also hosted on this repository. These findings suggest that MPC can be adapted to accommodate varying risk levels of collisions, as well as provide a feasible solution for complex multi-robot systems. As social media becomes an essential aspect of contemporary life, its impact on society remains a subject of debate. The widespread use of platforms like Facebook and Twitter enables global connectivity, but it also creates concerns about their influence. One major issue affecting public discourse on these platforms involves hate speech, a toxic expression that harms vulnerable groups. In response to this problem, which has sparked numerous lawsuits, several countries have introduced automated hate speech detection as a potential solution. This classification task has gained significant machine learning research attention, with advancements motivated by social and legal implications. From a methodological standpoint, research on automated hate speech detection faces challenges due to its subjectivity, as human evaluations alone can't ensure the accuracy and transparency of machine learning models. This issue becomes particularly problematic when considering deep neural networks, which can mask the reasoning behind classifications. In this context, we present an understandable, two-stage classification approach for hate speech detection that leverages visual and linguistic information. Our system achieves high performance on established benchmarks and serves as a transparent alternative to current state-of-the-art methods that prioritize performance over understanding. Additionally, our analysis of numerical results and model visualizations provides valuable insights into the hate speech detection process. In a notable finding, our research highlights the significant representation error in linguistic features and the significant accuracy loss in visual models, which suggests that current techniques overemphasize performance over understanding. Furthermore, our investigation of model decisions reveals a lack of consensus among experts regarding the interpretation of linguistic features. This work highlights the importance of a balanced approach to machine learning research that prioritizes both performance and understanding. By promoting a more informed discourse, we believe that our research can contribute to addressing the social and legal implications of automated hate speech detection. Our proposed model and accompanying analysis have been made publicly available on our GitHub page at https://github.com/kr309/mmhisd. This research received funding from the Data Science Institute at the University of California, Santa Barbara. With the data science program's support, our research was able to tackle the complex issue of hate speech detection. In summary, our research focuses on the social and legal contexts of automated hate speech detection and the importance of understanding deep neural networks. Our proposed model is designed to ensure the transparency and accuracy of machine learning research, which we applied to a multi-modal hate speech dataset. Our research provides a framework for balancing performance and understanding in machine learning research and highlights the importance of informed discourse in addressing social and legal implications. Our research made possible the detection of hate speech that may have gone undetected due to its subjectivity

We explore the effects of different degree distributions in a model of inhibitory neurons using a type-I intensity-based model. Building on past work by Melillo et al., who analyzed an analogous model with a power-law degree distribution, we examine networks with various distributions, including a narrow, Gaussian degree distribution and multiple others derived from the stabilization parameter gamma. For gamma less than or equal to one, we identify a neuronal population that inhibits synaptic inhibition, while larger values of gamma enable the emergence of bistability, including oscillatory states. As gamma increases, the neuronal population transitioning to spiking activity expands, with a limiting case that mimics a complete network of inhibitory neurons. For gamma greater than or equal to two, the dynamics converge to a state where neurons fire in a regular, synchronized pattern. Furthermore, we establish that the neuronal population that spiking activity emerges from is determined by the degree distribution, with a secondary stability transition occurring for gamma greater than one. For gamma greater than two, the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a uniform inter-spike interval. For the degree distributions derived from gamma less than one, we observe oscillatory states, while larger values of gamma lead to synchronized states with a uniform inter-spike interval. For gamma equal to two, the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a distinct, finite inter-spike interval. Moreover, we observe that the system exhibits a transition to a synchronized state with a uniform inter-spike interval as gamma increases beyond two. These findings highlight the intricate balance between neuronal connectivity and dynamics, emphasizing the significance of considering the structure of neural networks. The analysis also provides insights into the mechanisms governing neuronal behavior, including the interplay between local inhibitory processes and global synchronization phenomena. Such insights are crucial for addressing the complexities of neural systems and designing neural circuits. The presented model serves as a versatile tool, encompassing a wide range of degree distributions, thereby facilitating the systematic exploration of neural synchronization in inhibitory networks. As such, our analysis is relevant to various neural systems, including those found in cortex, ganglia, and retinal processing. The system's behavior is also reminiscent of experimental observations in epilepsy, microstrip and superconducting quantum circuits. Moreover, our findings are particularly significant in the context of artificial neural networks and systems, where inhibitory neurons are essential for competitive mechanisms, and synchronization is crucial for information processing. Finally, our model is also applicable to biological systems, including the case of Staphylococcus aureus bacterial colonies where inhibitory interactions prevent competitive mechanisms

Current automated program repair techniques face obstacles repairing mutations that cause program crashes, which often require multiple fixes involving various parts of the program. To address this issue, we developed antagonistic patch synthesis, a novel repair approach that directly aims to find mutually exclusive fixes to address multiple program issues simultaneously. Through empirical evaluation, we compared three different repair strategies: searching for a single fix, exploring multiple fixes, and considering opposing fixes, demonstrating that the antagonistic strategy yields a higher success rate in repair and provides more diverse and understandable fixes to the program. The empirical study is supported by a new tool called antagonistic patch synthesis, whose source code is available for further research. The tool leverages genetic programming to represent program fixes as candidate patches and multiple runs of fix synthesis for a single program crash as opposing fixes. The genetic programming candidate patches were evaluated for correctness through static analysis and testing, via three different interfaces: the driver, the hook, and the hook driver. The evaluation shows that antagonist strategy works for different repair interfaces and outperforms other repair strategies. The genetic programming interface was evaluated for candidate patches diversity using three different metrics: population, generations, and fitness. The evaluation shows that the tool achieves a high success rate in repair and provides more diverse and understandable fixes to the program. The empirical study highlights several challenging issues that caused program crashes, which often require multiple fixes involving various parts of the program, such as data type mismatch, variable scope, and program logic. The study also highlights several program issues that could not be repaired through genetic programming due to the inherent program complexities. The study suggests several potential areas for future improvement of the repair technique, such as integrating domain-specific features in the genetic programming representation and exploring alternative search methods that can handle program symmetries. This paper introduces a data spectrum description for the generative iterative fitting classifier (GIFC) and uses it to define the GIFC's capability region. From the data spectrum perspective, the GIFC is initially presented as a countable collection of Bayes classifiers. Building on this, the work defines the GIFC's capability region as a set consisting of the training data and points that have a similar probability density to the training data. This region is then analyzed in detail, with a bound established on its volume and conditions derived for the boundary points. It is also demonstrated that the GIFC's capability region can be exactly identified in some situations, such as Gaussian distributions, while an algorithm for approximating it in practical cases is proposed and validated through experimentation on real-world datasets. Finally, the GIFC's classification performance is evaluated with the proposed capability region, with results showing that it achieves satisfactory accuracy on a range of datasets. All experiments are supported with accompanying code and data, posted on https://github.com/baizhao/GIFC- Capability-Region. Identifying the source of enhancement in nuclear equation-of-state (EoS) is a pressing inquiry within nuclear physics. This article reviews current understanding and presents novel findings regarding the topic, with a particular emphasis on exploring the role of light exotic nuclei in EoS enhancement. Three-dimensional (3D) flow investigations are leveraged to explore enhanced EoS through collaborative nuclear collisions. Utilizing state-of-the-art dynamic quantum models, 3D flow is simulated with diverse EoS based on nuclear density and symmetry energy parameters. These simulations reveal that enhancement in EoS results in diminished 3D flow. This property enables 3D flow to serve as an indicator for EoS enhancement. Moreover, symmetry energy affects nuclear flow more profoundly than density-driven EoS enhancement. Light exotic nuclei, primarily consisting of protons, are hypothesized to contribute significantly to the former scenario, whereas compact exotic nuclei, comprised of bosons like $\Lambda$ or other strange baryons, are expected to contribute to the latter scenario. Lastly, preliminary data from several facilities, including AGAT, FAIR, NICA, and RHIC, are discussed in terms of EoS enhancement through 3D flow. This phenomenon is anticipated to be studied extensively with forthcoming large-scale experimental facilities, such as CBM and sPHENIX. By modeling flow using 3-parameter EoS, we can identify a crucial turning point where flow dynamics are influenced by the transition point's melting temperature and critical point's density, allowing for an assessment of EoS enhancement through flow studies. This is particularly evident in medium-density conditions where enhancement in nuclear EoS prevails. This article is intended to provide a comprehensive overview of 3D flow as a novel tool to study the complex collision structure and EoS enhancement in nuclear physics. Light exotic nuclei play a pivotal role in the enhancement of low-energy EoS through 3D flow studies. Graph neural networks (GNNs), which extend CNNs to capture graph structure information, have been applied in various fields. This research considers using GNNs in wireless communication systems. We analyze GNN implementation in distributed transmission systems from both design and optimization perspectives. To effectively support a large number of wireless devices, we discuss using GNNs in device clustering techniques. Moreover, we examine how to incorporate GNNs in the physical layer of wireless communication systems. Due to the graph's influence on GNN inference, we consider distance metrics in different wireless communication scenarios and propose joint optimization designs within these frameworks. The existing literature mainly focuses on design, while optimization is addressed through common approaches such as backpropagation or established optimization methods for communication systems. This research focuses on optimization strategies for GNNs in the context of wireless communication systems. We propose and evaluate different optimization methods, which have not been extensively explored in this field. By addressing both design and optimization, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of GNN applications in wireless communication systems. We have also identified key challenges and opportunities for future investigation. The impact of wireless channels on GNN performance also requires further exploration. This research aims to establish a connection between GNN design in communication systems and existing communication system design principles, as well as to identify optimization methods that can benefit from established best practices in communication system optimization. By achieving these goals, we can leverage the strengths of both fields and advance our understanding of GNN applications in communication systems. We also discuss how to address common challenges, such as distributed inference and data privacy, when integrating GNN design and optimization with communication system principles. The outcomes of this research can contribute to both GNN-based communication system design and general GNN design, which have been widely explored in computer science. By developing a systematic understanding of GNN design in communication systems, we can evaluate the performance of GNNs in communication systems and compare them to those in other fields. The diversity of communication system design goals and requirements allows us to analyze the effectiveness of different GNN design choices and optimization methods. The diversity of wireless channels and device distributions also leads to diverse distribution clustering strategies, device densities, and data exchange patterns. This diversity provides opportunities to generalize GNN design and optimization across multiple fields and applications. The trend of homicides in large provinces of Latin America suggests an alarming rise.  This study examines the temporal and spatial dynamics of homicides in Goias, Brazil, across a 13-year period from 2002 to 2014, using monthly data.  First, researchers checked for autocorrelation and seasonality in the data, which indicated a need for a model that could accommodate time trends.  There were three main methods to determine cluster patterns in the data, including (i) a statistical test to identify regions with elevated homicide rates, (ii) a method to test for homogeneous homicide rates across sub-provinces, and (iii) a method to identify cluster patterns within these sub-provinces.  These analyses identified 20 clusters in Goias, spanning 13 years, which were then linked to their corresponding economic and law enforcement indicators.  Notably, a negative correlation was found between police presence and homicides, as previously expected.  However, homicide rates were not necessarily lower in areas with higher police presence but rather lower in areas that received greater funding for public security.  This suggests that effective security measures can indeed lower homicide rates.  Furthermore, a positive correlation was found between unemployment and child homicide rates, indicating that economic instability can have severe consequences for vulnerable population groups.  Interestingly, a male-biased homicide rate disparity was observed, with younger individuals being disproportionately affected.  When comparing urban and rural homicide rates, a slight increase in homicides was found in rural areas, which may be linked to a lack of effective security measures in these regions.  These findings have significant policy implications, particularly with regard to urban and rural development strategies.  It was also observed that a low level of investment in social programs during the examined time period contributed to higher homicide rates in Goias.  Therefore, to mitigate this issue, public investments should be directed towards education and social welfare services in order to foster economic growth, reduce inequality, and provide better opportunities for vulnerable population groups.  These investments can have a significant impact on reducing homicide rates in Goias, similar to the positive outcomes observed in other contexts.  To support data-driven decision making, a model was developed that can predict homicide trends based on observed cluster patterns, providing valuable insights for policymakers and law enforcement officials.  This can be particularly useful for identifying areas at high risk for homicide and developing targeted prevention and intervention strategies. Stochastic Gradient Descent variants have become the go-to optimization choice for deep learning due to their superior performance and ease of implementation and tuning. Consequently, a wide array of optimization strategies has been developed, with researchers often overlooking the conditions under which these variants are supposed to excel. As a result, whether an optimization strategy actually improves training is heavily dependent on the specific data and initial conditions and may not live up to its supposed advantages, especially when applied to heterogeneous datasets. Furthermore, researchers have not thoroughly investigated when and why certain optimization strategies are supposed to perform better or worse than basic SGD. To resolve this, we have performed an in-depth analysis of the theoretical underpinnings of SGD variants to develop a unified framework for their evaluation and to create a comprehensive evaluation plan, which we have then applied to a range of optimization strategies, resulting in a ranking of their performance that is both theoretical and empirical in nature. By combining our analysis with a vast experimental database, we have developed a predictive model that estimates an optimization strategy's effectiveness based on the dataset and its characteristics, allowing us to develop accelerated versions of stochastic gradient descent that are adaptive to both the dataset and its training progress. These findings are then applied to a selection of state-of-the-art mini-batch SGD variants, resulting in the identification of factors that are favorable to their performance and the identification of circumstances that could potentially improve their performance. Ultimately, we have developed optimized variants of stochastic gradient descent that are accelerated and adaptive to both the dataset and its training progress. Our results indicate that optimization strategy performance can be improved by taking into account its supposed conditions of excellence and that a range of theoretical and empirical factors may have a negative impact on its effectiveness. By leveraging a comprehensive evaluation plan and empirical data, we have developed a predictive model of optimization strategy performance and created accelerated and adaptive variants of stochastic gradient descent that are optimized for a range of scenarios. These optimized variants are available for download at https://github.com/auriville/accelerated_sgd. They can be used within training scripts by replacing the standard SGD with the optimized variant of your choice, as illustrated in the accompanying repository. Our optimized variants are based on the numerical analysis and empirical findings presented in this paper, as well as other related research, as can be seen on the website https://optimization.ai. Our goal is to empower the community to develop accelerated and adaptive optimization strategies that are tailored to specific datasets and training progress, ultimately leading to improved training outcomes. A compactised version of MADEX, in the form of BabyIAXO, is being considered to analyze the characteristics of $^8$Li produced during double-beta decay processes. This would allow for a comparison with $^7$Be produced in the same experiments, resulting in valuable insights into the operation of astrophysical processes within the sun. Moreover, alongside its existing MADEX counterpart, BabyIAXO would be capable of generating extensive datasets, collectively offering sufficient statistics within a few years. Consequently, in a scenario where both experiments run concurrently, it's feasible that they'll be able to establish whether the $^8$Li double-beta decay is facilitated by a mechanism involving neutrinos or one that doesn't involve them. Moreover, it's possible they'll be able to determine the nature of the process's Hamiltonian, enabling scientists to validate the neutrino-related interpretation of the data by comparing it to different solar models. Furthermore, if the results indicate that neutrinos are involved, it would imply that high-energy neutrinos are generated by the sun but fail to detect them, a consequence of the so-called 'gambit.' In this paper, a discussion on the potential significance of the results is offered, along with the consequences of a neutrino-related interpretation of the data over the results obtained with MADEX. In the process, it's also considered whether the results could shed new light on outstanding questions such as the 'gambit,' the solar concentration factor, and the nature of astrophysical processes in general, as well as the creation of $^7$Be in sun's matter. In doing so, it's also explored whether MADEX is capable of detecting the high mass fraction of the process not mediated by neutrinos, and whether it's possible for MADEX to establish the nature of the neutrino-related Hamiltonian, a creation of nature that's not replicable in the lab. Our work also lays the groundwork for further exploration of KEYS models in extreme value theory. A key factor for robotic manipulation is the grasp planning, with a well-known challenge being the grasp synthesis failure for novel objects. One obstacle is the limited grasp dataset, particularly those tailored for robotic execution. In response, we introduce DexGraspNet - a comprehensive dataset of dexterous grasps suitable for robotic application, collected through simulation. Notably, our dataset stands out with its inclusive nature, encompassing diverse object categories and grasping hands, amounting to over 700,000 grasp poses that robotic algorithms can directly utilize. Additionally, our work includes a novel grasp dataset evaluation, focusing on assessing algorithms from a robotic perspective. Lastly, our website provides access to the collected data, along with guidance on replicating the collection process. In doing so, we aim to contribute to the advancement of robotic grasping and may ultimately contribute to the development of larger grasp datasets. A novel, motion-correction enabled four-dimensional T2-weighted turbo spin echo (T2w4D) sequence has been developed for increased scanning efficiency in abdominal regions. This technique employs a unique combination of a low-resolution target model sequence and a high-resolution velocity-encoding (VE) sequence to rapidly acquire MR images and subsequent corrected images through a more efficient, motion-averaged approach. In total, 2-3 acquisitions are required for a complete 4D data set. A target model sequence is used to identify the optimal time for data acquisition during breathing cycles and to adjust the sequence timing. A database of patient-specific target models is also proposed to improve sequence efficiency in clinical settings. This technique has been successfully tested in 15 patients and has provided high-quality, single-breath-hold MR images for abdominal computed tomography (CT) replacement. Our results demonstrate that the new sequence can provide superior image quality in comparison to traditional sequences, at least equal diagnostic quality, and improved sequence efficiency. This paper presents the sequence and its clinical application in abdominal scanning. A related, open-source project has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/berndt/poldi. This sequence has also been added to the IBM knowledge base as "4D T2-weighted turbo spin echo with motion correction for improved diagnostic information and reduced scan time in abdominal computed tomography replacement MR at 1.5 T". To bridge the gap between resource-limited and capable models, we develop a novel knowledge distillation approach that preserves data flow. This method accelerates the model compression process by leveraging the intrinsic data pipeline of the pre-trained teacher model. Our proposed framework, InDistill, uses a teacher-guided heuristic to assign weights for each feature score at test time. Notably, this framework is scalable and can be applied to various tasks, including vision and language, even without explicit attention mechanisms. Our experimental results on ImageNet, CIFAR-100, and GLUE benchmarks show that InDistill outperforms existing model compression methods, particularly in terms of latency and accuracy. For instance, it compresses ResNet-101 to match the accuracy of MobileNet-V2 with a significant improvement of 3.8% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet. The topological similarity of two surface foliations is defined as the existence of a homeomorphism between them and their respective product functions, when these functions are viewed as maps from the plane to itself. Our study focuses on two product functions derived from smooth submersion functions f and g over the plane P. Generating concise yet informative text is a crucial challenge in natural language processing. To address this issue, we propose a new approach using abstractive condensation that employs pre-trained language models to both understand and generate text based on provided prompts that evolve over time. As these prompts grow, they influence the model's understanding of specific concepts, allowing it to develop new and more detailed ideas over time. We tested this method by instructing a model to generate abstract summaries of lengthy academic papers, comparing its performance with both a pre-trained language model and a more sophisticated transformer-based algorithm. While the pre-trained language model was able to generate effective summaries, our proposed approach was found to produce the most natural, informative, and concise results, with a significant improvement in its ability to avoid repetitive summaries. Furthermore, human evaluators reported that the proposed approach led to the most improved understanding of the summaries' content. When asked to generate abstracts from random text, our proposed approach was found to produce the most coherent and natural results, surpassing not only pre-trained language models but also other sophisticated algorithms as well. Overall, our proposed approach demonstrates the potential to produce high-quality, concise, and natural language summaries automatically. It can be utilized in a web-based demonstration at https://abstrac.comprima.org/ and the code can be accessed on https://github.com/abstrac-comprima. Additionally, the pre-trained models used in this research can be downloaded from https://huggingface.com/abstrac-comprima. To facilitate easier integration of this method into other systems, we have made available a pre-trained model that is specifically designed to work with external knowledge sources, available at https://abstrac-ep.comprima.org/. Several key parameters for this model, including its training data and objectives, are outlined in Supplement C. Moreover, we have developed a set of tools designed to automate planning for abstractive condensation, available at https://planning-ep.comprima.org/. To access various other web-based tools related to this research, including a Condensation Playground, please visit https://playground.comprai.org/. Lastly, the report in figure form can be found at https://report-fig.comprai.org/. This challenge stems from the ice's surface boundary condition being subject to calving pressures, which can be described by a non-linear variational inequality influenced by a potential function. This potential function's graph is a convex, monotone, and continuous function, with a moderate growth rate. Employing the penalty method with a parameter-dependent term allows for the conversion of this non-variational inequality into a semicoercive variational inequality. This inequality must be solved in conjunction with a non-penetration constraint. To address this, a novel task called Simultaneous Robotic Structure (SRS) Service has been developed to maintain the system's underlying structure throughout control applications. By reinterpreting the problem as a control service, searching for robust solutions becomes necessary, and we introduce a new service framework to provide such solutions. However, recent advancements in monocular depth estimation techniques suggest an alternative form of unsupervised pre-training that doesn't require labels from segmented data. Although depth estimation isn't directly related to segmentation tasks than classification, we still explore their differences by comparing performance in unsupervised pre-training for segmentation. We created over 50 million synthetic images and put forward a novel network architecture capable of training on both depth and segmentation tasks simultaneously. We also conducted an ablation study that compares monocular depth estimation and classification to assess any residual effects and whether depth estimates offer benefits. The results from multiple experiments indicate that monolithic depth estimation does indeed provide better pre-training for segmentation than classification, as demonstrated by significant improvements in segmentation accuracy and model generalization on the Cityscapes dataset. Furthermore, we found that training on synthetic data alongside a simulator mask results in better performance than training without these masks. When applying our approach to real-world scenarios on the KITTI dataset, we achieved state-of-the-art results, outperforming previous approaches by a substantial margin. The code and datasets used throughout this research are now publicly accessible. We believe this contribution can aid the development of future unsupervised pre-training methods for segmentation. Additionally, we found that training on synthetic depth maps leads to over-smoothing of edges in depth maps, which in turn affects performance. We discovered that this issue can be mitigated by incorporating the original color information into depth estimates.
