Producing human-like text in dialogue requires sophisticated linguistic abilities, which can't be achieved by simply generating text from a database. Current methods fall short because they lack a deeper understanding of dialogue's complex structure. To make progress, we've developed LEATHER, a framework for written dialogue that separates content from structure and includes multiple sources of linguistic guidance. We've combined LEATHER with a large dataset to create improved generative models that produce more accurate results in multiple evaluation categories. By improving the coherence and consistency of generated text, these models outperform the best previous methods in all tested metrics. Notably, they even surpass human performance in one measure of coherence. To facilitate future research, we've released LEATHER and the enhanced dataset, along with detailed analysis and new evaluation tools, to help bridge the gap between current methods and true human-like dialogue writing. With these advances, we're one step closer to developing a linguistic genius that can outdo human writers in dialogue composition.

An online survey with 500 participants was conducted to determine how ordinary people, along with enthusiastic and casual users of the Signal app, interpret endpoint authentication methods (e.g. challenge-response authentication). The results showed that only 13% of Signal users could accurately explain the purpose of an endpoint authentication method, highlighting a potential issue with the app's design. The findings also indicated that even enthusiastic users may not fully grasp the security concepts they promote in public, and that casual users may have limited understanding of security practices despite their willingness to use the Signal app. The data shows that users are likely to comprehend an endpoint authentication method if they are given simple, clear, concise, and relevant information about it. The recommendations from this study aim to improve Signal's design by enhancing usability and understanding among ordinary users, and ultimately aiming to strengthen users' overall secure communication experience. The survey can be replicated with a broader scope to gather more insights from a more diverse user base, and could also be adapted into a within-subjects design to compare users' comprehension before and after an educational intervention. Many languages differentiate nouns based on grammatical gender, influencing how related nouns are represented in space. This paper examines the impact of grammatical gender on word embeddings, using Danish as a test case. Unlike prior studies, our investigation doesn't solely focus on inflected embeddings; instead, we also explore how the monomorphic form of Danish nouns is embedded. Our results show that changing the grammatical gender of a Danish noun, while keeping its meaning constant, significantly affects its embedding both when the noun is inflected and when it's in its basic form. Furthermore, we discovered that these changes can be predicted based on the noun's ending. This discovery led us to propose a new set of parameters for word embeddings that accurately represents a noun's different forms. Our experiments also reveal that Danish embeddings are often clustered by grammatical gender and, to a lesser extent, meaning. Moreover, co-occurrence data can be ineffective in capturing a noun's consistent meaning across different grammatical forms. Finally, our investigation shows that including monomorphic data in training can cluster related concepts together, including those with varying grammatical genders, drawing a connection between linguistic morphology and neural embeddings. The full dataset, including both inflected and monomorphic Danish embeddings, is available online. Our research raises important questions about designing word embeddings that can effectively capture language's intricate structural complexities. It also highlights potential dangers in modeling a single form of a variable, rather than accounting for its different grammatical instantiations. Last but not least, our investigation reveals that neural networks can learn and preserve a language's intricate morphological features, even when these are undistinguishable in surface form. They can also achieve this without relying on explicit training objectives related to morphology. Interestingly, our findings show that neural networks, capable of modeling a variable's different forms, can't always infer its variable status from the input without prior knowledge. They can also produce unwanted clustering by form, even when trained to do otherwise. We establish new property $\tau$ rigidity results for certain arithmetic groups.  First, we show that arithmetic groups with certain symplectic representations that have a specific rigidity characteristic are also rigid.  Second, we prove that certain arithmetic groups with maximal representations that have a specific rigidity characteristic are also rigid; this proof relies on a technical calculation involving Bruinier-Williams-Feldman series.  We also use numerical analysis methods to study the stability of Bruinier-Williams-Feldman series and provide an alternative approach to a long-standing conjecture in the field.  In addition, we provide examples of "charmable" but "rigid" arithmetic groups with non-scalar centralizer actions and give conditions under which "charmability" implies "rigidity" in certain cases.  Finally, we provide examples of "charmable" arithmetic groups with noncompact Zariski closures and outline an approach to proving "charmability" in general such cases.  Our results rely on combinations of geometric, algebraic, and analytic techniques as well as heuristics.  Our work has the further goal of motivating and providing the background for a conjecture in the introduction.  This paper is a companion to a separate work by the author.

Estimating the pose of objects in still images is a complex problem that
has not been fully addressed. While significant advancements have been made,
it continues to be a challenging task, especially for intricate objects. In
contrast to pose estimation in videos, where temporal context is available,
still-image pose estimation relies solely on the visual data. Existing methods
that calculate pose in still images often require large amounts of annotated
data but try to compensate by using 3D object detection results. Our novel
approach focuses on class-level pose estimation, predicting the overall 3D pose
structure of an object class rather than the detailed pose of individual
instances. Since class-level pose estimation cannot be directly learned from
image data alone, we introduce a method that utilizes text-based class
descriptions to initialize the learning process. This text information serves
as a starting point for zero-shot learning, where we explore different
strategies to separate pose estimation from other visual classification tasks.
Our experiments on the YCB-benchmark dataset demonstrate that our method can
effectively calculate the overall 3D pose structure of objects from novel
categories without any additional training data. Additionally, our findings
reveal that our approach performs better when compared to models that require
positional signal from image data for training. Our code is available on
GitHub at https://github.com/alexander-lenz/zero-shot-pose-estimation. While
our current implementation is limited to English language descriptions, we
believe that our method can easily be adapted to other languages by using
machine translation tools. Our results suggest that zero-shot pose estimation
can be a valuable starting point for further research and, combined with other
techniques like online data collection, potentially lead to more robust and
generalizable methods. Our empirical analysis of the role of language and
number of training examples indicates that there is still a significant
gap between current still-image pose estimation techniques and those used for
video pose estimation. Ultimately, we hope that our work will contribute to

Predicting future traffic is crucial for urban city planners. However, the task is challenging due to a lack of data. Current approaches rely on sampling data from traffic networks, but this limitation restricts their effectiveness. There's also a significant information overlap in traffic networks, which is currently underutilized. Inspired by the efficiency of point-of-interest similarity-based recommendations in online services, this research aims to improve sparse traffic forecasting by leveraging similarity in traffic networks. Initially, this is achieved by extracting features from traffic networks using a self-attention mechanism that identifies patterns. Next, traffic forecast predictions are generated by combining the extracted features with historical traffic data using a neural network. Finally, a neural tensor decomposition approach is employed to optimize network flow and minimize data requirements. Experiments conducted on real-world traffic data demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method, outperforming existing sampling-based techniques. Analysis of performance highlights the importance of similarity-driven components within the overall approach. Interestingly, key features identified through this method align with established traffic modeling theories, such as the fundamental diagram of traffic flow. This research showcases the potential benefits of applying similarity-based recommendations in transportation modeling. It further contributes to the existing body of work by developing an open-source framework for traffic forecasting. This framework has the potential to support broader research into traffic flow dynamics. Importantly, the proposed method does not rely on additional sensors or infrastructure and can be adapted for use in cities worldwide with varying geometric and attributive characteristics. This research expands on existing knowledge in transportation science and machine learning literature. Finally, the paper includes a discussion on potential future directions, including the integration of traffic forecasting and flow control systems. This research provides valuable insights for city planners and policymakers, highlighting the significance of accurate traffic forecasting in informing urban transportation strategies. Blazars with high energy radiation in the MeV-GeV range typically exhibit an excess in their spectral energy distribution above soft X-ray levels, which some objects cannot naturally reproduce through Compton scattering. This exclusion might be overcome if the scattered photons were polarized to some degree, as a secondary scattering off free electrons in a magnetized plasma could provide sufficient radiation above soft X-rays. Census data is a vital source for small-area statistics in many countries, particularly those with low and high-income nations. This research compares the performance of three estimation techniques using Brazilian census data: a design-based approach, model-based estimation, and two robust regression models. Estimation methods were applied to three variables: a binary, an ordinal, and a continuous variable. This analysis used secondary data from the 2010 Brazilian Census, including information from both the individual microdata and the aggregated summary data. A simulated design with 1000 replications was employed to compare the performance of these estimators in terms of bias, precision, and reliability. Results indicate that model-based estimators outperformed others when estimating mean values, while a different estimator performed better for binary variables. This study also found that, in most cases, a simple linear regression model performed poorly in unreliable municipalities. Conversely, a more robust regression estimator performed well across all scenarios, providing consistent results and performing relatively well in terms of precision and reliability. Ultimately, this study recommends the adoption of this model-based estimator for large areas but notes that additional research is needed to explore alternatives for binary variables. It also suggests exploring strategies to improve linear regression performance in certain municipalities. This research utilized computer software and a simulated environment to compare the performance of different estimators, providing actionable recommendations for statistical agencies in low and high-income nations. This approach enables the bettor to represent their initial wealth as a density matrix. Our study indicates that a subsequent bet, based on a post-measurement state, can be viewed as a quantum version of the standard Kelly wager, provided the initial state is classical. We investigate this quantum wagering strategy at both the level of the individual bet and within a repeated betting scenario, obtaining the maximum asymptotic growth rate per bet. Our findings also suggest a relationship between this quantum wagering strategy and the original Kelly wager. We further extend these results to a scenario where the quantum state is dynamically evolving according to a quantum Markov process. We conclude by examining a scenario in which a bettor's evolution operator may be unphysical, leading to an increase in asymptotic growth rates per bet. Time series data with multiple periods poses a challenging modeling task due to inherent uncertainties and noise, often masked by simplifying assumptions in existing research. This study tackles this issue by developing a novel generative model, MPTSM, as a variational Bayesian approach. By treating parameter frameworks as complex distributions with uncertain means and sparse diagonal covariance matrices, MPTSM distinguishes itself from standard models by incorporating uncertainty and sparsity within period-dependent parameters, yielding a scalable and efficient model. Using the Bayesian variational inference framework, MPTSM derives a stochastic gradient variational algorithm that minimizes reconstruction error and KL-divergence. Experimental results on artificial and real-world datasets show that MPTSM surpasses state-of-the-art multi-period time series models in prediction accuracy, especially in sparse scenarios. Furthermore, MPTSM exhibits superior scalability and efficiency compared to existing multi-period models, with computational advantages of O(T^(1.05)P) and O(T^(1.15)P) respectively. This study contributes a versatile generative model for multi-period time series modeling that accurately captures uncertainty and sparsity, outperforming existing research in both performance and wall-clock time. The model and associated inference algorithm are now openly accessible on GitHub, facilitating future developments. The empirical findings highlight the significance of uncertainty sparsity in multi-period time series modeling. The study also sheds light on its practical implications and offers avenues for further investigation. The empirical results indicate that the stochastic gradient variational algorithm performs well even with a relatively small number of iterations, achieving convergence in around 10-20 iterations in multi-period time series modeling. The model's wall-clock time is directly proportional to the expected value of length and period. The computational advantages are largely attributed to the use of the conjugate gradient solver for Cholesky and KL-divergence. The model's scalability and efficiency can be further improved by employing distributed computing and parallel processing. The study reveals that the MPTSM model exhibits desirable performance on a wide range of multi-period time series datasets, with the most challenging instances being sparse and irregular time series. The study also shows that the MPTSM model can be used as a flexible and general-purpose time series forecasting approach that can be extended to various applications. The study's empirical results reveal that the MPTSM model surpasses state-of-the-art time series models in artificial and real-world datasets, with the largest performance gains observed in sparse and irregular time series. This led to the logic being expressed in terms of Baire or Hilbertian logic, with a sublogic known as steadfast logic standing out for its weak comprehension principles. This approach leverages task-specific constraints and kinetic energy rewards, where the user interacts with the system, and we collect resulting data. Subsequently, we employ a constraint-based reinforcement learning method to design an optimal control policy. To facilitate robust learning, we introduce the problem of finding the most informative trial under uncertainty, taking into account the system's stochastic dynamics and our prior knowledge. A new optimization method is developed to solve this problem, along with a distribution-free algorithm that yields a practical solution. When applied to the simulated quadrotor, our approach results in stable flight within a short period of time, where the user is presented with a live interface. Computational simulations are carried out to verify the method and evaluate its performance. This research investigates Steklov eigenvalues for nearly spherical domains.  Initially, we present a method for calculating these eigenvalues in full spherical domains, which is then adapted for nearly spherical domains with non-empty, closed boundaries.  For nearly spherical domains that are concave or convex, we establish the essential features of these eigenvalues and demonstrate their dependence on the domain's boundary characteristics.  Furthermore, we calculate the eigenvalues for specific nearly spherical domains: half spheres, spherical wedges, parabolic cylinders, and hyperbolic cylinders.  Our method also enables the determination of eigenvalues for general spherical domains at their extremities.  This research introduces new essential Steklov eigenvalues for nearly spherical domains that do not possess these eigenvalues.  For instance, a convex spherical wedge possesses an infinite number of these eigenvalues, as does a hyperbolic cylinder.  By employing our method, we can calculate these eigenvalues explicitly.  This research also addresses an open problem posed by J. Jost and Z. Zhang regarding the existence of non-trivial Steklov eigenfunctions in convex spherical wedges.  Lastly, we calculate the eigenvalues for half spheres, spherical wedges, parabolic cylinders, and hyperbolic cylinders, which serve as examples of nearly spherical domains.  Our method enables the determination of these eigenvalues in a limiting case where the domain's boundary approaches a closed, non-empty subset of a sphere.  This research introduces new findings regarding the behavior of these limiting domain's eigenvalues.  For instance, a sequence of parabolic cylinders with increasingly narrow cores demonstrates that these limiting eigenvalues may vanish.  Using our method, we can calculate these limiting eigenvalues explicitly. In the context of power network expansion, the European Commission issues non-binding guidelines that member states must consider when requesting funds for new infrastructure. This study focuses on the methodological aspects of the ERGOM model, which is used to assess requests for funds made by member states. This model incorporates the Commission's guidelines into two distinct optimization problems that are used to evaluate various performance indicators. One optimization problem is a chronic investment model that determines the optimal network configuration given existing transmission capacities, while the other is an acute investment model that determines the network configuration that minimizes costs under given transmission capacities. The Collatz Conjecture remains an unsolved problem in the field of mathematics, originally posed by Lothar Collatz in 1930. It presents a sequence of numbers starting with any given n and follows a specific set of rules: if n is even, it is divided by two, and if it's odd, it's multiplied by three and then added to the number 1. Interestingly, researchers have found that regardless of the initial value, this sequence eventually reaches the number 1, and they can demonstrate this for nearly all numbers within a reasonable timeframe. However, proving this pattern for every single number, without any exceptions, has been a persistent challenge that has left the Collatz Conjecture as a renowned unsolved problem. Many mathematicians believe it is a fundamental problem and many key theories rely on its solution. If proven, it wouldn't just confirm the Collatz Conjecture's truth, but it would also have significant implications on the broader mathematics community. Many mathematicians have compared its solution to a 'Rosetta Stone' that could unlock various areas of mathematics. Historically, some of the most influential mathematicians including Stanislav Smale and Neil Sloane have made efforts to solve the problem, using number theory as their approach. Smale hypothesized a key finding - if n is odd, it must be divisible by three - which, if proven, has profound consequences. Smale's hypothesis aligns with his 1986 statement, and many mathematicians have made similar assumptions. However, Smale's hypothesis remains unproven to this day. This paper will focus on an alternative and unproven hypothesis: if n is divisible by five, it must be divisible by the number that comes after it. Dividing the conjecture into this simpler hypothesis using a different approach may help in finding a solution to the broader problem. This paper will present a test of this new hypothesis on a vast range of numbers from 1 to 400, and it will also include a test against Smale's previous number, 52, which is according to his 1986 statement. Specifically, we investigate the performance of quadratic measurements in obtaining the optimal signal estimation through means of mutual coherence and condition number. We show that for a k-sparse signal, applying quadratic measurements can yield an optimal condition number of O(k^2) in various settings, with specific instances including quadratic, linear, and Fourier measurements. Furthermore, we provide numerical experiments to support our theoretical findings. Interestingly, the analysis reveals that signal sparsity plays a pivotal role in the complexity of the optimization problem involved, with a decrease in sparsity leading to a decrease in the condition number. We also discuss how our results are complementary to those obtained using linear measurements, particularly by indicating that there is no faster restoration algorithm than the currently known one. Finally, we outline the limitations of our findings and suggest potential areas for their application, including the solution of non-convex matrix completion problems. This leads to intricate patterns of laser-induced diffraction in liquids with high nonlinearities and scattering indices. Notably, this often results in complex diffractal structures not typically observed in gases. However, the exact thermal profile development during these processes remains unclear. In our research, we employed high-speed imaging to visualize the lateral thermal diffusive profile within the liquid during the entire duration of intense laser-induced reactions. This revealed that the primary mechanism of thermal self-induction in liquids involves the straightforward scattering and subsequent forward scattering of pump light by the generated nonlinear waves. High-speed data processing requires an adaptable system for managing large-scale analytics pipelines. These pipelines integrate various processing stages that analyze and interpret data streams and historical databases in sequence. However, current distributed programming frameworks are ill-equipped to handle the complex task of coordinating data processing across different stages, especially when some operations fail, leading to slowed execution and increased costs. To address this challenge, we introduce H-STREAM, a novel framework for building analytics pipelines that allows for easy configuration and rapid querying of data processing pipelines. H-STREAM leverages a graph data model to represent each processing stage as nodes and their interactions as edges, enabling efficient failure recovery and optimization. By testing its performance with real-world data, our framework has shown significant cost savings and faster processing times of up to two orders of magnitude compared to existing frameworks. Our framework's innovative querying capabilities have enabled a two-second response time for processing and querying a graph. Furthermore, we observed that stream processing times are as fast as 0.1 milliseconds per node, while querying graph distances takes 0.05 milliseconds or less. These results make H-STREAM an efficient and powerful tool for building analytics pipelines that can be further optimized. Our framework is available for open access and collaborative development. It includes an API for stream processing and querying data that mirrors the widely-used Apache Storm API, facilitating adoption and improvement by the distributed systems community. Our framework's source code can be found at https://github.com/berndrunk/h-stream, with Bernd Ortgies serving as the primary maintainer. Our framework's public data sets, test results, and execution plans can be accessed at https://h-streams.appspot.com/. Our study has received funding from the National Science Foundation, award IIS-2166092. Our framework's work aligns with the goals of the NSF program 'Harnessing the Power of the Cloud through Cloud-Enabled Computing, Networking, and Storage' by leveraging cloud resources for improving data processing and querying outcomes. Our framework's work also supports the objectives of the NSF program 'Toward Maximizing the Quality of OAG in Large-Scale ANOVA Contexts for Sustainable Applications’ by enabling scalable data analysis and decision-making. Our framework's work has implications for the 'Smart City' initiative by supporting efficient data processing and querying for enhancing the quality of life for citizens. Our framework's improvements in data processing and querying can benefit the 'Digital Civil Rights' initiative by improving decision-making for law enforcement and judicial purposes. We have conducted comprehensive direct numerical simulations (DNS) and high-order numerical simulations (HNS) to determine the energy spectrum of inertial wave turbulence within a quadrupolar flow structure. By defining a critical radius as one-tenth of the container's dimensions, we analyzed the energy spectrum within this region and found it to conform to the Kolmogorov spectrum. Our analysis also revealed the spectral exponent to be in precise agreement with theoretical predictions from Kolmogorov and Zakharov-Kolmogorov, displaying minimal variability with respect to the critical radius. Furthermore, we observed consistent exponents across both DNS and HNS in tandem with our previous findings. To enhance the generality of our results, we undertook additional simulations (3D-6DE) to investigate the energy spectrum in three-dimensional flows with external rotation. These simulations not only validated our previous findings but also yielded identical exponents in 3D-6DE cases, thereby substantiating the universality of the inertial wave turbulence energy spectrum. For reference, all raw data from these simulations are publicly available through the link hpcpublicdata.github.io/TK-Spectrum-Data. As such, our comprehensive study affirms the general applicability of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov energy spectrum in a diverse range of flows. This research was supported by the National Science Foundation. To facilitate the assessment of its impact, a detailed report is provided at hpcpublicdata.github.io/TK-Spectrum-Report. Additionally, relevant metrics are tracked using the Software Sustainability Alliance's Metric Catalog. With the goal of enhancing transparency and reproducibility, all publicly available data and the report are accompanied by usage guidelines. To gauge user interest, a related question on the Assessing Software Quality for Reproducibility in High-Performance Computing survey has been included. Upon completion, the response will be added to the response dataset maintained by the Software Sustainability Institute. Lastly, all data and the report are concurrently archived. Please note that further details on the computation are available at hpcpublicdata.github.io/TK-Spectrum-Computations.

Detecting redshifts in high-z sources such as quasars and galaxies is critical in millimeter and submillimeter observations. We introduce 'High-z Sudoku,' a interactive redshift estimation tool for millimeter and submillimeter spectra. By leveraging a customizable grid of possible redshifts, High-z Sudoku enables users to estimate a quasar's redshift based on its millimeter or submillimeter spectrum. We estimate a 90% confidence interval for the correct redshift value, accounting for 10,000 simulations. The accuracy of the grid-based method and the associated 90% confidence interval are examined across a range of scenarios. We show that a 21-point grid produces a 90% confidence interval width of around 0.0035 (or 40 km/s) when there is no noise involved. Adding typical millimeter-wave noise to the spectrum results in a 90% confidence interval width of around 0.13 (or 190 km/s). However, if at least five millimeter-wave data points are available, the 90% confidence interval width decreases to around 0.07 (or 100 km/s) for a 21-point grid. We test High-z Sudoku on millimeter and submillimeter spectra of seven high-redshift quasars that had previously estimated redshifts through the use of ultraviolet data. Numerical research on the J1-J2 Heisenberg model, which features a half-integer spin on the triangular lattice, focuses on the intermediate J2/J1 range where local structure factors indicate ordered and liquid phases due to local symmetry disruption. By analyzing spin fluctuations at the minimum of the energy's imaginary part, we identify the onset of symmetry disruption. Near this transition, the spin correlation length exponentially decreases and pseudo-critical behavior emerges, which is more pronounced in the liquid phase at higher J2 values. This transition in the pseudocritical behavior shifts back into the ordered phase as J2 increases, potentially transforming into a first-order transition in certain parameter ranges. Further investigation into the liquid and ordered phases reveals a hard spin-liquid that persists in a substantial portion of the J2/J1 parameter space. In contrast to previous findings, our research shows the absence of a nematic spin-liquid and a possible reentrant spin-liquid phase that occurs when J2 exceeds 0.38. This reentrant phase may also exist within the ordered phase at lower J2 values. Lastly, our research suggests that the ordered and liquid phases in the model exhibit distinct dynamical signatures, which can be extracted through the minimum of the energy's imaginary part to determine the ground state's configuration. By numerically computing this quantity, our research confirms that the ordered and liquid phases coexist in the model and that their relative proportions in the J2/J1 parameter space can be quantified. In particular, our research indicates that the ordered phase dominates at lower J2 values, while the liquid phase emerges and eventually becomes prevalent at higher J2 levels. This ground-breaking work could potentially shed new light on the recent findings from the experimentally studied NaYbO_2, which features a similar J1-J2 Heisenberg model and exhibits an ordered ground state with nematic properties due to local spin nematic disruption in the higher J2 region. However, our research reveals that the model exhibits a significant difference from the experimentally studied case, which occurs when J2 exceeds 0.18. At this point and beyond, the ordered ground state transforms into a liquid one, which may also underlie the experimentally observed homogeneous broadening in the NaYbO_2 sample's infrared absorption modes. This potential connection to the experimentally studied case, along with the significant results obtained, make our research highly relevant and potentially influential in the study of frustrated magnets, particularly in the case of the NaYbO_2 material and related systems.

A new kinetic model, the speed-dependent Soret kinetic model, has been developed to analyze rarefied gas dynamics by taking into account variations in collision frequency across different molecular speeds. This model's performance is evaluated through comparisons with direct numerical simulations and Monte Carlo molecular dynamics simulations. Specifically, the model's predictions regarding temperature and velocity distribution fluctuations are examined in various scenarios, including anisotropic flow in a heated channel and steady-state flow in a planar channel. By calibrating the model's collision frequency using thermal conductivity data from Monte Carlo simulations, the model's accuracy is demonstrated for a hard-sphere interaction scenario. Furthermore, the model's capability to predict non-Maxwellian velocity distributions at low molecular speeds is reported, along with an exploration of the impact of collision frequency discrepancies on gas dynamics, particularly in cases of weakly heated channels. Lastly, the models' predictions for non-equilibrium Onsager coefficients have been verified against the results of Monte Carlo simulations. All of these findings support the notion that the speed-dependent Soret kinetic model is an effective model for capturing the effects of intermolecular potentials in rarefied gas dynamics, particularly in situations where collision frequency varies across molecular speeds. This model's performance is particularly strong in scenarios involving slow molecular speeds, where it outperforms traditional models based on the Boltzmann collision model. Nonetheless, at high molecular speeds, the model's performance is comparable to that of a Boltzmann collision model. Ultimately, the model's accuracy in predicting temperature and velocity distribution fluctuations makes it a valuable tool for further research into the development of optimized surfaces for various applications. These applications include thermal management systems, microfluidic devices, and other technologies related to the manipulation of fluids and heat. This resource serves as a central location for the model's documentation, code, and data, allowing users to access and contribute to the model as needed. After adjusting for beam efficiency, we found that NGC 5253 produces 6.9×10^38 W of H30α emission, indicating that approximately 3.2% (or 0.64 Z_sun M_sun/yr) of its gas is converted into stars. Utilizing different H30α correction factors, we found that NGC 5253's gas depletion times range between 0.56 to 0.89 blr (in 10^8 years), which is shorter than in the SMC. Our study discovered that a linear relationship between the H30α correction factor and metallicity does not exist, as the H30α correction factor in NGC 5253 is lower than in the SMC. These results imply that a revised, galaxy-specific approach for H30α correction factors is necessary, especially in the case of NGC 5253. Our study also suggests that a 20% (or 0.2 Z_sun M_sun/yr) rate of supernova feedback from a 35 M_sun/solar-type star is insufficient to account for the gas consumption rate in NGC 5253. Our final findings support further observations of NGC 5253 to clarify the relationship between the H30α correction factor and metallicity. Additionally, our study encourages the use of ALMA's H30α observations in the study of star creation measures in low-metallicity galaxies. Finally, our data illustrate the potential for using ALMA's H30α observations to analyze the properties of nearby galaxies. Temporal knowledge graphs are gaining prominence as an effective data model that enables the capture and querying of events unfolding over time. They are utilized in diverse link prediction tasks such as identifying individuals' relationships, forecasting future events, and determining their locations. Many current approaches for link prediction in temporal knowledge graphs are reactive and reconfigure their models or loss functions for every time slot, which is inefficient and causes implementation difficulties. In contrast, our static model approach in this paper involves developing a static graph framework using temporal knowledge graphs. This model leverages novel node and link representations that combine temporal and spatial context to accurately model relationships in temporal knowledge graphs. To achieve this, we employ a two-pronged representation method that uses a shared latent space to capture temporal context and spatial graphs to capture node relationships. This model also uses a novel score aggregator that combines node and edge representations to predict links in temporal knowledge graphs. We tested the static model approach in three scenarios, including point-to-point, multi-hop, and location association link forecasting tasks, utilizing datasets from Wikipedia, Wikidata, and DBpedia. The results show that our static model approach exhibits remarkable performance, surpassing various baseline methods, including graph embedding and temporal models. Notably, it demonstrates an average increase of 11.6% in performance over the top-ranked baseline method, the HRECA model. This research provides a static model approach in temporal knowledge graph learning that is effortless to implement and can be adapted for various link forecasting tasks. It also identifies the optimal static model architecture with a prune aggregator that attains exceptional performance, opening up new avenues for link forecasting in temporal knowledge graphs. The static model approach in this paper can be utilized in diverse social network and information retrieval applications, such as social network analysis, search query optimization, and more. While SNE predicts links in information networks effectively, its time complexity relative to network size (N^2) can be prohibitive for larger networks. To improve this, we present SSNE, a scalable variation of SNE that uses sparse matrix operations to predict links in large networks efficiently. SSNE achieves this by representing nodes as vectors that capture their characteristics, allowing predictions to be made without considering individual edges in the network. SSNE produces predictions based on a score function that compares the similarity of node pairs based on their relative proximity in the network, thereby outperforming other methods, such as node degree distribution, in predicting links. Our analysis of SSNE reveals key factors that influence its accuracy, such as node degree distribution and network density, providing a framework for its application. SSNE has significant potential to expand SNE's applications to massive information networks that were previously out of reach due to its computational limitations. SSNE's performance outperforms other methods, such as node degree distribution and reverse nearest neighbors, in predicting community structure in various real-world networks, such as web networks and citation networks. While SNE and its variations, such as SSNE, exhibit exceptional performance in predicting links and community structure in a range of real-world networks, their capabilities to predict community structure in a graph are limited to graphs that have at least a minimum density. Therefore, SNE and its variations are not suitable for predicting community structure in sparse graphs. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel transformation of the adjacency matrix that captures the core characteristics of a sparse graph, such as its low density and degree distribution, to convert it into a denser network while maintaining key statistical properties. This enables us to apply SNE to sparse graphs that cannot be predicted by SSNE, outperforming other methods, such as node degree distribution and reverse nearest neighbors, in predicting community structure in these graphs. Our analysis of this transformed SNE reveals key factors that influence its accuracy, such as node degree distribution and minimum degree. Additionally, we develop a distance metric that can be used for any graph, including sparse graphs, to predict community structure in a range of real-world networks, such as web networks, citation networks, and clinical networks. This metric outperforms other methods, such as node degree distribution and reverse nearest neighbors, in predicting community structure in these networks. Finally, potential hurdles and obstacles need to be addressed when operating such marketplaces, with a view towards their potential adoption in real-world applications. This chapter serves as an introductory resource for those seeking to implement blockchain technology in decentralized marketplaces, covering essential concepts, from technical to regulatory perspectives. To understand performance issues, developers need to know where bottlenecks arise, and for this, they often rely on existing profiling tools. However, to address abuses of certain software, a different approach is needed - one that not only looks at how a component is used but also at its results. This study examines the performance anomalies of the Python crypto module. By analyzing real-world applications, such as GitHub projects and Pypi packages, we looked at how they employ functions within the crypto module. Furthermore, we assessed the security implications of these best practices by analyzing real-world security incidents and relevant security reports. Our findings are based on two large datasets: a comprehensive collection of real-world applications' source code from popular repositories (1.7M unique files), and corresponding executable code from binaries (13M unique files), all traced back to 2019. Our results can contribute to both more effective performance optimization and enhanced security for the crypto module. They raise important questions about the current tools for detecting security issues and how they might be improved. Additionally, our work highlights distinct patterns in how real-world security incidents make use of crypto functions, contrasting with what we saw in performance analysis. Finally, our results underscore the significance of considering both practice and consequences when evaluating certain practices, leading to a more nuanced understanding of these practices. Most urban settings are equipped with intelligent navigation systems like GPS, which provide geospatial data with geotagged points of interest. However, many cities lack detailed and comprehensive mapping data. To address this gap, we present VALUE, a novel framework that leverages crowdsourcing and machine learning to annotate city environments efficiently. Our method relies on a voting system to detect meaningful urban features in geotagged images. A deep learning model then generates a semantic layer for city maps by classifying geotagged points into distinct categories such as buildings, roads, and parks, based on the computed feature maps. VALUE's performance on the NTU Freeway map dataset outcompes existing methods, demonstrating its effectiveness and scalability in annotating urban settings. The framework's source code is available on GitHub at the specified repository.

In seismic reflection imaging, infrared thermal data analysis, and other fields, sparse signal patterns are frequently encountered. Various $l_p$-norm based methods have been developed in response to these patterns, with a focus on their mathematical formulation. However, the use of these methods is often hindered by the lack of a clear indication about which $p$-norm to choose and the computational cost associated with it. In this study, a unified framework called NuSPAN is presented, which addresses these challenges by learning a proximal point system from data through a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). A suitable combination of learned indicators and computational methods is then applied to seismic reflection inversion. Results from numerical experiments show that NuSPAN outperforms traditional sparse methods in terms of inversed image quality and computational efficiency. Additionally, the potential of NuSPAN is explored in other applications where data-driven sparse pattern analysis is required. A novel quantum error correction approach, the concealed inverses protocol (CIP), is introduced to address quantum errors in a specific type of circuit, the linear Pauli circuit (LPC). The CIP utilizes a specific basis known as the Wilson basis, effectively eliminating errors caused by quantum fluctuations within the apparatus. By using CIP on a superconducting quantum circuit, we investigate how this scheme can correct errors resulting from various types of quantum fluctuations, specifically focusing on two distinct scenarios: when a single type of error is prevalent and when multiple types of errors coexist. By applying CIP to these scenarios, we find that it is capable of effectively correcting errors under both conditions. Furthermore, we investigate how CIP performs when subjected to different levels of errors and find that it is capable of correcting errors with a high level of accuracy, known as logical fidelity, exceeding 99% regardless of the specific type of error. Notably, CIP performs consistently well when a single type of error is prevalent, with logical fidelity exceeding 99% for errors less than 9%. CIP also demonstrates the ability to correct errors resulting from multiple types of errors, with logical fidelity exceeding 99% when errors exceed 10% but fail to exceed 98% when errors exceed 90%. Lastly, CIP is capable of adapting to different levels of errors, with logical fidelity exceeding 99% when errors exceed 90% and failing to exceed 99% when errors exceed 100%, indicating its robust performance across a wide range of scenarios. Overall, our findings demonstrate the ability of CIP to effectively correct errors in a variety of scenarios, making it a promising candidate for superconducting quantum computing. Future research plans are outlined at the conclusion of this study. This implicit assumption can lead to subpar performance when dealing with images taken from unique vantage points, such as those captured from the top or bottom. By decoupling orientation variability from our proposed OCN, we've observed improved accuracy in image classification tasks, particularly when dealing with scenarios involving flipped and rotated images. Through comprehensive testing on various datasets, we've found that the OCN outperforms traditional ConvNets in orientation invariant image classification. To enhance the precision and speed of industrial robots, a cost-effective method for upgrading existing models involves integrating additional sensors.  This research aims to improve motion control in old robots by using accuracy-enhancing sensors, but due to inaccuracies in their calibration and physical properties, this poses an optimization problem.  A proposed solution involves incorporating the readings of these extra sensors into a control strategy based on the smoothness of the motion.  A key aspect of this approach involves defining a quantifiable measure of the smoothness of the motion that can be used to optimize the parameters of the additional sensors.  This research also examines the challenges and limitations of the method, demonstrating its potential for improving the precision of the motion.  A physical test was conducted on a KUKA KR150-2. The results show that the method can reduce the smoothness error by up to 50% and the position error by up to 20% in specific scenarios.  Although the method has its drawbacks, its applicability and effectiveness in upgrading old industrial robots make it a valuable tool for the industry.  A comparison with other accuracy-enhancing methods highlights the advantages of this particular strategy.  This research was conducted as part of a collaboration between the University of Genova's Department of Naval Architecture and the KUKA company's technical development team.  A related patent application was filed in May 2017.  The research's limitations and future avenues for exploration are also discussed.  Specifically, the method's sensitivity to noise in the additional sensors' readings could be better characterized and addressed through the incorporation of a robust estimation technique, such as an algorithm designed to provide reliable estimates in the presence of uncertainties.  A potential area of future research could involve the development of a more in-depth mathematical analysis of the method's limitations and its application to specific industries and use cases.  The current implementation of the method assumes a fundamental model of planar motion, and its application to three-dimensional motion could be a valuable area of further investigation.  The method's current simplicity also presents opportunities for further exploration.  A potential approach could involve the development of a more sophisticated version of the method, either by incorporating additional physical properties of the additional sensors or by by optimizing a different performance metric, such as the position of the end effector.  This research's findings suggest that the method could be used in a variety of performance criteria and its application to specific industries and use cases could be a valuable area of further investigation. Traditional statistical analysis methods for repeated observations are geared toward understanding short-term variations, but many medical research questions require a long-term perspective. This paper focuses on the individual-level data that arise in such cases, featuring multiple event occurrences that may be censored. Given that many health issues are multi-faceted and influenced by various risk factors, a practical approach is to model different disease states as interconnected entities. Building on this concept, a novel method is introduced that assesses multiple states, taking into account both transitions between states and individual differences in this complex process. An additional development provides a detailed framework for this modeling, enabling the exploration of various factors that may contribute to disease progression. The method is illustrated using data from the Stockholm Myocardial Infarction Register, focusing on the multiple pathways to a patient's first myocardial infarction. A novel approach called the Multi-Site Quadrature method is introduced to efficiently linearize the molecular continuum by approximating electron integrals with a limited set of determinants. This method divides electron integrals into site-specific components based on their proximity to atomic centers, enabling a deterministic linear approximation. Furthermore, it capitalizes on the inherent low-rank structure of these components to determine optimal coefficients. In contrast to traditional linearization methods, MSQ excels at minimizing the approximation error, especially for complex molecular integrals where neighboring atomic contributions are significant. The performance of MSQ is demonstrated through extensive benchmarking of all-electron energies, accurate to millijoules per electron, while requiring a substantial reduction in computational time compared to conventional methods. The method is thus well-suited for scaling modern quantum chemistry algorithms without compromising accuracy. The MSQ source code has been made available for public use. For connected finite graphs, we examine the transition probability matrix of random walks. Assuming the eigenvalues are ordered such that the first eigenvalue is greater than or equal to the others, we show that the second-largest eigenvalue in relation to the graph's size is a sufficient indicator of a spectral gap. We provide a polynomial expression for this second-largest eigenvalue in terms of the first few eigenvalues and the order of the matrix. This holds true for generic matrices and bounded matrices. We verify that this polynomial is distinctive for distinct random walks on connected finite graphs. For special cases, including matrices related to Cayley graphs, circulant matrices and q-circulant matrices, we present distinct polynomial expressions based on the group of affine automorphisms generating the matrix. We generalize our findings to matrices related to graphs. The distinction of these polynomials confirms the non-isomorphism of these matrices and, consequently, the non-isomorphism of the corresponding graphs. This result generalizes to matrices related to semi-simple Lie algebras. We apply our methods to characterize the matrices related to odd-dimensional rotation groups. We use our results to determine when random walks on these matrices are asymptotically uniform. Furthermore, we show that the canonical basis of the adjacency matrix of a connected graph is not an eigenbasis, unless the graph is a bipartite clique or a cycle. We address a related open question posed by Diaconis. Our methods involve connections to invariant operators, irreducible representations, characteristic polynomials, Chevalley's theorem and Higman's criterion for nilpotency. We also utilize Schur's polynomial and the Newton-Girard identities to achieve our goals. The distinction of polynomials arising from random walks on graphs has significant implications for problems in cryptography, algorithm design and computer science, as we illustrate with examples. The distinction of polynomials arising from irreducible representations of symmetric groups provides an alternate proof of a theorem regarding the non-isomorphism of permutation groups, as applied to the cases of $A_{n+1}$ and $B_n$. Additionally, the polynomials arising from tensor powers of irreducible representations of dihedral groups have a distinct form that facilitates classification of the polynomial map in Galois theory. We conclude with an open problem related to polynomials arising from deformation theory in algebraic geometry. In computing science, a widely adopted technique for breaking down complex problems into manageable parts is the use of recursive definitions.  However, programmers often encounter difficulties in containing recursive definitions within mutually recursive groups, as each element typically shares dependencies with others.  
We have proposed an innovative approach to addressing this issue by employing a timed model for recursive definitions, allowing a definition to be instantiated only after a predetermined minimum threshold of related definitions has been met.  This method offers a considerable level of flexibility, accommodating various scenarios, such as single or multiple recursive definitions, as well as situations where certain definitions are skipped or delayed.  A formal proof of the timed model's soundness has been established using a high-order logic theorem prover, demonstrating its potential applications in a wide range of domains.  This concept is illustrated through a case study in abstract state machines, specifically the creation of an abstract representation of pushdown systems, utilizing a timed model to capture the accepted languages of finite automata combined with a pushdown process.  This study highlights the benefits of the timed model in simplifying the process of breaking down complex problems into manageable parts, similar to how data types are typically structured.  Pushdown systems serve as a foundational model for a broad range of programming concepts, including stack-based programming, object-oriented programming, algebraic data types, and others. This research investigates novel optical nanoantennas with distinct and intriguing properties, which can also find applications in emitting light. By examining and understanding electromagnetic eigenmodes in carefully designed nanostructures, we can exploit their unique characteristics. Specifically, we analyze a hybrid dielectric-plasmonic nanoantenna with remarkable unidirectional light emission capabilities, high luminosity, and enhanced interaction coupling. Our approach involves analyzing electromagnetic eigenmodes using quasi-static and full-wave electromagnetic simulations. By decomposing these eigenmodes into their dipole and higher-order multipole components, we can quantify their inherent emission properties. Our results demonstrate that electromagnetic simulations provide a complete description of the electromagnetic eigenproblem. Ultimately, we identify conditions under which these nanoantennas exhibit stable, unidirectional, luminous light emission. Moreover, we demonstrate that these nanoantennas can emit light coherently, realizing conditions that may enable their utilization in emitting light. Despite language technology advancements, hate-speech remains a significant issue on Indian social media, with severe consequences such as mob violence and even murder. Existing research has primarily focused on English-based datasets, leaving Hindi and Bengali to cope with ineffectively designed classifiers that often mislabel posts, exacerbating the problem. To address this, our investigation employs a novel dataset, HATE SPEECH IN HINDI-ENGLISH (HATE20) and HATE SPEECH IN BENGALI (HATE11), testing the efficacy of CNN, LSTM, and attention-based models to identify hate-speech and assess their performance across varying training data sizes. Our results reveal that a well-trained model's accuracy declines significantly when confronted with unseen data, underscoring the need for more research in hate-speech identification for under-resourced Indian languages. Moreover, we observe that under circumstances of limited training, a model's performance may improve when introduced to new, unseen domains with additional data, highlighting the possibility of transfer learning's success. In space exploration missions, low-mass detectors like thin gas chambers are used for detecting weak neutrino interactions. These interactions typically result in only a fraction of an GeV in energy output, and recoil particle tracking is essential for making accurate projections. Gas Time Projection Chambers (GTPCs) have the capability of not only identifying the energy released, but also the mass and charge of the recoil particle, thanks to 3D tracking. However, the overall system's performance is limited by the technology's sensitivity to the direction and energy of recoil particles. This is particularly true when working under conditions where ionization yields vary due to system dependencies. By introducing novel observables that account for ionization energy, recoil particle direction, and energy, it is possible to enhance detection sensitivity. This can be achieved by the integration of machine learning algorithms and advanced ionization energy modeling, and is particularly beneficial for the detection of particles with very low energies. This study focuses on the development of these new observables and their application in the context of GTPC's GEM-based architecture. As part of this research, two simulated scenarios are examined. First, the detection of minimum ionization particles like cosmic rays at various energies is investigated. This is followed by the simulation of weakly ionized particles such as those produced by neutrino interactions on argon nuclei. It is found that the use of these new observables, along with the integration of ionization energy modeling and machine learning algorithms, significantly improves the detection of particles with very low energies. This research demonstrates that machine learning algorithms are particularly effective at distinguishing between recoil particles with very low energies, and that the use of ionization energy modeling along with time-projection technique can significantly enhance detection capabilities. These improvements are expected to be highly beneficial for upcoming missions that rely on the detection of very weak neutrino interactions. These include the future Oumuamua-like missions that aim to study this unique object, and a conceptually similar project such as the proposed SPUMS mission. This research has significant implications for various space-based missions that aim to detect very weak neutrino interactions. We establish a concept of geodesic motion in the manifold formed by a Gaussian random field. The shortest paths, determined by minimizing the variance, have a linear trajectory, further characterized by a closed-form analytic solution valid for all finite variance. This is made possible by a stochastic version of the Pythagorean theorem that enables breaking down the minimizing path into independent components. Additionally, we demonstrate the independence of each branch point in the generating function of the Gaussian field's Laplace transform, implying an infinite set of variational reproducing kernel particle methods, enabling faster computation, as the number of particles can be arbitrarily high. In the one-dimensional case, this results in a variant of the Laplace solver with a time complexity of $\mathcal{O}(N/\log{N})$, where $N$ is the number of particles. Moreover, we outline the generalization of our findings for multidimensional Gaussian fields, along with the initial application to the study of Brownian motion, including a novel method for rapidly constructing mini-sampling trees. Finally, we utilize the stochastic wave equation to derive the generating function of the Laplace transform of the one-dimensional Gaussian field. The resulting method enables approximating arbitrary Gaussian fields given the correlation function, with an approach analogous to variational Monte Carlo in machine learning. The empirical performance of our algorithms is investigated by employing correlation functions from various domains, including financial, medical, climate, physics, and genetics data. We demonstrate that our methods outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches, with a notable improvement in computational time. The implementation details can be found in the provided repository. We also present an interactive framework for visualizing the generative process of a Gaussian random field featuring a browser-based interface. This is made possible by a innovative approach to hierarchical transform domain sampling, with potential applications in machine learning. The concept and methods have been successfully communicated and showcased in a recent TEDx talk. The current research was inspired by a conversation with the artist Tomás Saraceno, with support from the CERN & Art and the Swiss Embassy in Buenos Aires. The work was further advanced in a recent artistic collaboration with the artist collective Heath Bunting, with ongoing research and development guided by a new prototype for artist-prisoner collaboration, with the goal of applying our methods in socially transformative projects. The work has been recognized with the Swiss CTI Innovation Award in Artificial Intelligence, with a special mention at the 2022 Concordia Challenge at the Concordia Summit. The researchers have successfully disseminated their research to the general public through presentations

In this research, we have investigated the localization patterns that emerge in a complex system connected in the center. The system's density distribution and its fluctuations have been analyzed as key indicators of localization. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, we have examined both the finite-size scaling of the system's density fluctuations and the growth of density correlations across the system as a key benchmark for understanding localization patterns. The results show that when the system is in a non-localized state, its density fluctuations scale in a typical manner with system size, but this scaling behavior changes significantly when the system transitions into a localized state, where density fluctuations become less dependent on system size and instead exhibit a scaling that is consistent with logarithmic growth. Furthermore, in the localized state, density correlations across the system are found to increase at a logarithmic rate, which is in contrast to the non-localized state, where such correlations typically decay at an exponential rate. These findings are further supported by calculating the system's density distribution as a function of distance from the center of the system and by inspecting the graph structure. Previous studies have demonstrated that supervised learning techniques can be applied to detect Multiple Sclerosis lesions with high accuracy. Nevertheless, existing methods train and test using the same dataset, neglecting the fact that new data and updated labels become available over time. To address this, the goal of our work was to segment lesions when moving across multiple clinics and process sequential data with increasing labels and features. We developed a novel approach, the Continual Learning-based Multiple Sclerosis lesion Segmentation (LMS) method, to achieve this goal. This approach combines the Continual Learning strategy with a Multiple Scales feature extraction technique to initially segment lesions before refining them using a supervised approach. We evaluated LMS using multiple datasets, including the MSSEG17 challenge dataset and two newly established datasets from Drexel University and Temple University, all featuring axial T1 post-contrast MR images. The results showed that LMS achieved superior performance compared to traditional methods when using the MSSEG17 challenge dataset and demonstrated efficient segmentation across various clinics with improved accuracy. To facilitate the reproduction of our research, the source code, dataset, and pre-trained models for LMS have been made publicly available. We also successfully demonstrated the application of LMS in a real-world setting, using the model to detect lesions at Drexel University before fine-tuning it to accurately segment lesions at the University of Pennsylvania. This work has the potential to contribute positively to both the medical field and the machine learning community by addressing the issue of segmentation in the presence of shifting data distributions through the use of the Continual Learning approach. Moreover, LMS expands the capabilities of lesion segmentation to multiple clinics and hospitals, opening up new possibilities for both research and clinical use. We believe that our work sets a solid foundation for future research in the detection and segmentation of MS lesions across various clinical settings and data distribution shifts. Furthermore, LMS presents an efficient solution for segmentation in the absence of data augmentation. Ultimately, the goal of our work is to develop a robust and efficient segmentation algorithm that can effectively detect lesions across multiple clinics and distribution shifts, paving the way for seamless use in both clinical settings and competitive challenges. To the best of our knowledge, LMS is the first approach to accomplish segmentation in the absence of data augmentation and Continual Learning-based MS lesion Segmentation across multiple clinics and distribution shifts. We hope that our work will inspire future research in the detection and segmentation of MS lesions as well as the machine learning community. The primary contribution of our work is the development of a robust and efficient segmentation algorithm that can effectively detect lesions

The origin of the diffuse gamma-ray background is still unknown, with extragalactic gamma-ray sources offering key clues. If the gamma-ray emission from galaxy clusters is widespread, it could explain the gamma-ray background, given the right spectrum and intensity. To investigate this possibility, we examined gamma-ray data from 12 clusters, focusing on the spectrum and intensity, by modeling the emission using a broken power law. Our results suggest a universal spectral index of α=1.48 for low-energy gamma-rays and a high-energy cutoff at the TeV range. However, if we assume a broken power law, it would require a steeper high-energy index, α=2.17, which would result in excessive gamma-ray emission from clusters, far exceeding observations. This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a specific logarithmic weight given by $\log\left(\frac{2k}{1-x}\right)$ over the interval $(-1,1)$ where $k>1$, and we derive the weights of an associated orthogonal set of polynomials through a transformation involving the Chebyshev polynomials of the first and second kind. This enables us to calculate the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients and evaluate the asymptotic behavior of orthogonal polynomials. Furthermore, we prove that the polynomials' asymptotic behavior can be represented as a perturbation of the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind. This is achieved by applying the steepest descent method in a novel manner by deforming the type of a singular integral from which the orthogonal polynomials are obtained. This integration technique yields a simple result, and we utilize additional methods to handle cases where the deformation leads to singularities. Moreover, we calculate the asymptotic degree of the orthogonal polynomials and verify the uniqueness of the orthogonal polynomials through the uniqueness of the associated differential equation. We support our findings with numerical examples by calculating the asymptotic recurrence coefficients for various values of $k$ and evaluating the polynomials' convergence for $k=2,3,5$ and $k=\frac{7}{3},\frac{13}{3}$. Lastly, we derive an expression for the polynomials' norm asymptotics as given by P\'{o}lya. This expression is applicable to a broader range of weights that are logarithmic types near the endpoints of their interval of definition. Text-video retrieval has gained significant attention due to the potential for advanced multimedia search. Current methods primarily rely on three-pronged strategies of embedding matching, combining, and ranking to resolve text-video alignment, feature fusion, and similarity calculation. We examine the superfluid properties of a model involving spin-orbit coupled bosons in a optical lattice. The interplay between a uniform magnetic field and lattice modulation gives rise to a modulated superfluid with spatially varying phase and spin density wave order. As the modulating frequency changes, particularly at low dimensions, the modulated superfluid experiences phase transitions and instability thresholds. Applying a thermal analysis, we investigate the impact of thermal fluctuations on these quantum phase transitions, first through the mean field approximation and then incorporating quantum and thermal fluctuations using a bosonization method. They were asked to compare'stinky' instances with actual failures, rate their detection difficulty, and whether they've encountered such issues. We also discovered stinky failures are generally considered easy to identify, yet hard to address. These results suggest that indicating bugs is a priority for developers, and they are capable of detecting stinky failures relatively easily. We introduce Profound, a novel method for independent robot navigation, and
evaluate it using an ActiRobot on real-world indoor routes. Profound leverages
active inference algorithms to determine the robot's optimal self-motion in
pre-learned environments via Markov Decision Processes. Notably, Profound's use
of variational active inference allows the robot to autonomously decide when
to plan ahead, enabling a more energy-efficient trajectory. When compared to
traditional sampling-based navigation methods, Profound demonstrates a
considerable 50% reduction in computational expense. Furthermore, ActiRobot
tests reveal that Profound results in a 23% decrease in navigation time. Our
results demonstrate the potential for variational active inference algorithms
like Profound, to empower robots with a deeper understanding of their surroundings.

We introduce the Box Re-Ranking (BRR) method for mitigating false positives in domain-adaptive pedestrian detection. By incorporating detection information, BRR employs an adaptable Siamese network to distinguish person boxes and suppress non-person boxes. Unlike traditional domain-adaptive methods, BRR doesn't require a paired dataset and is effective even with limited annotations. Experimental results on the Citypersons and Veillette datasets show that BRR achieves a false positive rate reduction of 20% with only 10 annotated images for fine-tuning, outperforming a strong baseline with extensive 3000 annotated images. Moreover, BRR performs comparably to state-of-the-art domain-adaptive methods when paired with a pedestrian mask. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. With this approach, pedestrian detection models can be more robust and reliable on unfamiliar domains, reducing the impact of domain disparities. We also investigate the effectiveness of re-ranking boxes alone, demonstrating its ability to reduce false positives in domain adaptation and its potential as a valuable processing stage in practical applications. Our analysis also highlights that domain adaptation methods can be used to mitigate a condition known as label noise. Although originally intended for tackling changes in data distribution, domain adaptation methods can be used to address label noise as well. We found that domain adaptation methods can improve performance by as much as 8% when the training data contains noise, making them a valuable tool in practical machine learning scenarios, and further research is recommended to discover other applicable domain adaptation methods for addressing label noise. They were the first to provide a direct link between $R(\xi)$ and the Riemann invariants $r_1$ and $r_2$, yielding the formula $R(\xi)=e^{2\theta_0} \exp(-2\int_{\theta_0}^{\theta} \sigma_3 d\tilde{\theta}}$ where $\theta$ is expressed in terms of $r_1$ and $r_2$, and $\xi$ is a reference wave number. Notably, for small $|k|$, the reflection coefficient can be approximated as $R(\xi)=1+\frac{2(1+2k^2)[r_1(\xi)+r_2(\xi)]_+}{3\sqrt{1+r_1(\xi)_+r_2(\xi)_+}}+O(k^3)$. This formula is the highest order of accuracy obtained so far in physical space, providing a direct link between the reflection coefficient and the Riemann invariants. The goal of text categorization is to maximize an accurate text classification result. To achieve this, a text categorization system consists of two components: a text representation module and a classifier. The text representation module converts words or characters into a fixed-length vector representation called documents, which are then used by the classifier to perform classification. Traditionally, text representation modules utilize a fixed set of vectors (dictionary) to represent documents. However, this approach has a weakness in that it can only utilize a fixed set of vectors, which limits its performance. On the other hand, varient models can learn and update the dictionary dynamically, but they have a weakness in that they are prone to overfitting. To overcome these challenges, we have developed a new type of text representation module called sibylvariant, which dynamically changes the set of vectors used for document representation. Additionally, we have introduced a new method for regulating the degree of change in the vectors, which enables the sibylvariant module to achieve better generalization performance. Experimental results have shown that the sibylvariant module outperforms traditional text representation modules in terms of accuracy and F-measure. In the ultrastrong light-matter coupling regime, we investigate the interaction of a two-level system coupled to an electromagnetic field within a cavity. This investigation reveals novel stabilization techniques for matter states within a cavity. Within the context of a scenario involving electron scattering, we demonstrate that vacuum Rabi modes can exert a influence comparable to a Lorentzian potential, protecting metastable matter states against vacuum decay through a Rabi-induced avoided crossing. The competition between light-matter coupling and electron scattering leads to an optimal condition for matter state stabilization, which is quantified by an enhancement factor. This research paper presents a method for training four-legged robots to efficiently use spring-based actuators for locomotion. We introduced a novel elastic actuator model to account for its nonlinear dynamics in force and displacement. We formulated the movement strategy using the concept of task space, taking into consideration the complex factors. Additionally, we developed a new learning approach for the policy using neural networks and quadruped-specific architectures to utilize the spring-based actuators' capabilities during movement. The method was successfully tested on a simulated robot named Sqima, built with a Harvard Baby Actuator. The simulation results show that our task-based elastic actuator model is accurate and that the trained policy leads to substantial improvements in energy efficiency, reducing fuel consumption by 50%, while maintaining comparable movement speed. The findings suggest that by incorporating spring-based actuators, quadruped robots can achieve increased speed and efficiency due to the ability to utilize the spring energy for propulsion. In a multi-hop home WiFi network, there are two types of devices: access points and extenders. Each home network consists of a main access point and several other devices, with the main access point usually being the master. To improve performance, we need to choose between using these devices as access points or extenders, and we've developed a tool to make this decision. This choice depends on the channel load and how devices are physically located, and we use the IEEE 802.11k standard to gather necessary information and adjust the network accordingly. By making this decision, we increase home WiFi throughput and reduce interference between different networks. Experimental results show that our method increases the median WiFi throughput by 25% compared to a random choice between devices. Furthermore, we found that using the IEEE 802.16n standard to measure signal strength in 60 MHz bands accurately predicts the optimal device choice, and we're within 10% of the best possible throughput with our current information. Finally, we found that using the IEEE 802.11v "Turbo Mode" helps maintain high throughput even when the network needs to restart, and we see a 5% decrease in median throughput when compared to a network with no frequency shifting. This suggests an opportunity to leverage this standard to improve performance in scenarios where the network needs to restart. While our method does not provide optimal performance in all cases, it performs well in a real-world implementation and offers a number of benefits, including reduced interference and increased throughput. This demonstrates an opportunity to improve the robustness of a WiFi network by making intelligent use of available standards, and we hope this work will serve as a foundation for future improvements in WiFi performance.
